## Background

Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major global health threat, causing an estimated 10.8 million new cases and 1.25 million deaths in 2023. It has re-emerged as the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent, surpassing even COVID-19 [1]. The burden of TB is heaviest in low- and middle-income countries with fragile health systems, especially in sub-Saharan Africa. In 2022, Africa accounted for about 2.5 million new TB cases and 424,000 TB-related deaths, representing over one-third of global TB deaths [2]. Ghana has experienced a worrying rise in TB cases; for example, 19,000 cases were recorded in 2023 though the World Health Organisation (WHO) projections is showing decreasing TB incidence in Ghana (130 per 100,000 in 2024) [1]. TB in Ghana continues to be a significant cause of morbidity and mortality, responsible for over 5% of all deaths annually in the country [3].

National TB program data show that from 2018 to 2022, Ghana recorded fluctuating TB treatment success rates between 78% and 88%, slightly below the global average of 88% in 2024 (WHO Global TB Report 2024). The case detection rate improved marginally from 36% in 2018 to 47% in 2022, yet this still falls short of the WHO target of 70% detection. TB mortality also remains high, with deaths often associated with delayed diagnosis, treatment default, and co-morbidities such as HIV/AIDS and diabetes mellitus [4].

HIV co-infection significantly complicates TB management in Ghana. Nationally, around 20% of TB patients are estimated to be HIV-positive, and this subgroup experiences poorer treatment outcomes. Diabetes mellitus, although less frequently reported, is increasingly recognized as a risk factor for adverse TB outcomes due to its immunosuppressive effects and potential interactions with TB medication [4].

Co-morbidities such as HIV/AIDS, diabetes mellitus (DM), substance abuse (alcohol or illicit drugs), hypertension and other chronic conditions pose additional challenges to TB control. These co-morbid conditions can worsen the course of TB and impede treatment success. HIV-infected individuals have a higher risk of developing active TB – an estimated 16–27 times higher than HIV-negative individuals [5] Global analyses indicate that TB treatment mortality in co-infected patients ranges from ~ 16% to 35%, compared to ~ 4–9% in TB patients without HIV [6].

Diabetes mellitus is another growing driver of adverse TB outcomes, given the increasing prevalence of type 2 diabetes in high-TB-burden countries. Diabetic patients have roughly a 3-fold higher risk of developing TB than non-diabetics, and diabetes can worsen TB disease severity and outcomes [7]. A systematic review reported that diabetes was associated with an ~ 1.9-fold increase in the risk of death during TB treatment and nearly 5-fold higher risk when controlling for other factors [7]. Biological mechanisms for this include diabetes-related immune dysfunction and possible pharmacokinetic interactions of TB drugs with hyperglycaemia or diabe8ic comorbidities. In Ghana, like many African countries, faces a rising diabetes prevalence alongside endemic TB, potentially creating a “double burden” that threatens TB control efforts [8].

Behavioural and substance use factors, such as alcohol abuse and smoking, are well-known to negatively influence TB treatment adherence and outcomes. Chronic alcohol use is associated with poor medication adherence, higher default rates, and liver toxicity on TB therapy [9]. Patients with alcohol use disorder have been found to be significantly more likely to default from TB treatment [10, 11]. Alcoholism and drug abuse also exacerbate poverty and reduce healthcare access, leading to delays in seeking care and increased loss to follow-up. A recent large cohort study in Europe found that alcoholism increased the odds of TB-related death by over eight-fold (OR 8.3) and substantially raised the risk of treatment failure [12].

Hypertension may not directly influence _Mycobacterium tuberculosis_ pathogenesis in the same way as diabetes or HIV, but its presence can indirectly affect TB outcomes through immune modulation, drug interactions, and comorbid cardiovascular risks [13].

In Ghana, several health system challenges continue to hinder effective TB diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up, particularly in rural and underserved regions. One critical issue is the shortage of skilled health personnel in rural areas, where TB patients often face delays in diagnosis and initiation of treatment due to the absence of trained clinicians and diagnostic infrastructure. Additionally, the supply chain for TB medications and diagnostic tools remains fragile, with frequent reports of stockouts and logistical bottlenecks that disrupt continuity of care. These supply chain inefficiencies affect not only first-line drugs but also laboratory reagents essential for bacteriological confirmation and follow-up testing [4].

Moreover, primary care facilities—where most TB cases are first encountered—are chronically underfunded, lacking both infrastructure and capacity to manage complex TB cases, particularly those involving co-morbid conditions like HIV and diabetes. This often results in late referrals to tertiary institutions, by which time patients may already be experiencing complications or advanced disease. Poor integration of TB services into the broader health system, limited community-based follow-up mechanisms, and inadequate patient tracking contribute further to loss to follow-up and poor treatment adherence. Addressing these systemic barriers is essential for improving TB outcomes and meeting national and global targets [1, 4].

Previous research in Ghana has reported TB/HIV co-infection rates around 11–23% in various regions, and treatment success rates nationally have remained suboptimal (approximately 85% in 2020) [4] amid challenges of drug-resistant TB and patients defaulting treatment).

However, there is limited data on how other co-morbidities (e.g. diabetes, hypertension, substance use) affect TB outcomes in the Ghanaian context, and which patient subgroups are at greatest risk of unfavourable outcomes (like treatment default or death).

The study was conducted at the Chest Clinic of the Korle-Bu Teaching Hospital (KBTH), Ghana’s largest national referral centre. Tertiary facilities often manage more complex TB cases, including patients with co-morbidities or advanced disease, making it an appropriate site for evaluating the impact of co-existing conditions on TB treatment outcomes. However, findings may not be generalizable to rural or primary care settings, which is acknowledged as a study limitation.

## Methods

### Study design and setting

This was a retrospective descriptive cross-sectional study conducted at the Chest Clinic of Korle-Bu Teaching Hospital (KBTH) in Accra, Ghana. KBTH is a large tertiary referral hospital that also serves as a national centre of excellence for chest diseases. The Chest Clinic provides outpatient and inpatient services for TB diagnosis and treatment, and it manages complicated TB cases referred from other parts of Ghana. The study targeted the period from January 2021 to December 2022, during which the hospital had fully implemented an electronic medical records system (Lightwave Health Information Management System, LHIMS) for TB patients. This timeframe was chosen to ensure data availability and completeness; TB case records before 2020 were less reliably captured electronically.

### Study population

The study population comprised all TB patients with at least one documented co-morbidity who registered for treatment at the Chest Clinic of KBTH between 2021 and 2022. According to clinic records, a total of 993 TB patients were managed in this period, out of which 258 had one or more co-morbid conditions recorded. The study included these 258 TB patients with co-morbidities in the analysis. Co-morbidity was defined as any additional diagnosed chronic condition alongside TB, such as HIV infection, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, substance use disorder (e.g. alcohol abuse), chronic liver disease, renal disease, malignancy, etc., as recorded in the patient’s medical notes. Both new TB cases and previously treated cases were included, provided they had a co-morbidity. Patients without any documented co-morbidity were excluded from this study.

### Data sources and collection

Data was extracted from the LHIMS electronic database and patient TB treatment cards. The parameters (TB, HIV, diabetes, hypertension, substance abuse etc.) were diagnosed using standard laboratory and clinical methods [1]. A standardized data abstraction form was used to collect relevant variables, including socio-demographic information (age, sex, marital status, level of education, employment status), clinical characteristics (type of TB – pulmonary vs. extrapulmonary, sputum smear/Xpert MTB status, HIV status, other co-morbidities), and] treatment outcomes. Co-morbidities were grouped into categories of interest (HIV, diabetes, hypertension (HTN), substance abuse, and others). “Substance abuse” predominantly referred to harmful alcohol use, as documented by clinic staff, but also included any illicit drug abuse if noted. The category “others” encompassed less common co-morbid conditions such as anaemia, malignancy, chronic malaria, chronic heart failure, chronic liver disease (including hepatitis B), mental health conditions, and other miscellaneous diagnoses (e.g., stroke, autoimmune disorders) that were each represented by only 1–2 cases.

The study recorded the specific outcomes of TB treatment as classified by the National Tuberculosis Control Program and WHO guidelines: Cured (completed treatment with documented bacteriological evidence of clearance, for sputum-positive cases), Treatment completed (completed therapy but without final sputum result); “Cured” and “completed” were combined as “successful treatment”; Defaulter (treatment interrupted for ≥ 2 consecutive months, now termed “Lost to Follow-up”), Died (death from any cause during treatment), and Treatment Failed (persistently positive sputum or clinically failed regimen). It was also noted if any patients had treatment stopped by clinicians due to severe adverse events or other reasons (this was recorded in a few cases). Additionally, for patients who defaulted, clinic records and outreach worker notes were reviewed to document the reasons for default as reported (e.g., lack of transport, adverse drug effects, etc.).

### Data analysis

Statistical analysis was performed using IBM SPSS (Version 26) and R (Version 4.3). Descriptive statistics were generated for all variables. Categorical variables (e.g. sex, co-morbidity type, treatment outcome category) were summarized as frequencies and percentages. Continuous variables like age were summarized by mean and standard deviation (SD) or median (interquartile range) as appropriate. The study population was stratified by co-morbidity categories and by key outcomes to facilitate comparisons.

The overall treatment outcome distributions (treatment success vs. defaulted vs. died vs. failed) was compared across the major co-morbidity groups (HIV, diabetes, hypertension, substance abuse, and other co-morbidities) using the chi-square test of independence. Given the small numbers in some outcome subcategories (e.g., only 1 treatment failure), the study focused on the three primary outcomes (cure, default, death) for comparison and considered “treatment failure” and “stopped” as rare events to mention qualitatively. Pairwise comparisons for specific outcomes of interest were conducted. Odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated for these comparisons, and Fisher’s exact test was used when cell counts were small. Tests with _p_< 0.05 were considered as statistically significant.

Additionally, predictors of treatment default were explored using logistic regression. The binary outcome was default (yes/no). The independent variables could influence adherence, specifically: age, sex, marital status, and presence of certain co-morbidities were included. Age was treated as a dichotomous variable (< 35 vs. ≥35 years) based on the observed association with default, and marital status was dichotomized as single vs. having a partner (married/cohabiting) for analysis. Given that no patients with diabetes defaulted, the diabetes variable in the regression model was not included to avoid complete separation issues. A backward stepwise approach was used to arrive at a parsimonious model. Adjusted odds ratios with 95% CI and p-values were reported for the final model covariates.

### Ethical considerations

The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Accra Technical University Research Ethics Committee with protocol identification number ATU/MLT/ET/003/2023–2024. As this was a retrospective record review, the need for informed consent from individual patients and consent for participation was waived by the Korle Bu Teaching Hospital Chest Clinic. All data were de-identified and kept confidential.

Every effort was made to ensure data accuracy and privacy. Only the research team had access to the raw data, which were stored on password-protected computers. In presenting results, the aggregate findings were reported without personal identifiers.

## Results

### Characteristics of the study population

A total of 258 TB patients (out of 933) with co-morbidities were included in the analysis as in Fig.1. The mean age was 44.3 years (SD ± 15.2), with a range from 15 to 85 years. The largest age group was 45–54 years (23.3% of patients), and 70.9% of patients were aged 25–54 (Table1). There was a male predominance: 156 (60.5%) were male and 102 (39.5%) were female, yielding a male: female ratio of ~ 1.5:1. Regarding marital status, 139 (53.9%) were married, 73 (28.3%) single, 28 (10.9%) divorced, 13 (5.0%) widowed, and 5 (1.9%) cohabiting. Most patients had some formal education – only 10% had no formal education, while 30% had secondary education and 23% had tertiary-level education. In terms of employment, 71% of patients were employed (formally or self-employed) and 10.5% were students. Pulmonary TB was the predominant form in this cohort; 201 patients (78.0%) had pulmonary TB, whereas 57 (22.1%) had extrapulmonary TB (lymphatic, pleural, spinal, or disseminated TB).

### Prevalence of co-morbidities

By design, all patients had at least one co-morbidity. Table1 shows the distribution of co-morbid conditions. HIV infection was the most prevalent co-morbidity, documented in 188 out of 258 patients, which is 72.9% of the study population (95% CI: 67.3%–78.0%). The next most common co-morbid conditions were hypertension and substance abuse; each found in 15 patients (5.8%). Substance abuse in medical records primarily referred to heavy alcohol use; a few cases also noted illicit drug use. Diabetes mellitus (mostly type 2) was present in 11 patients (4.3%). A variety of other co-morbidities were present at lower frequencies (collectively 11.2% when summed). These included four patients with anaemia (1.6%), three with chronic malaria (1.2%), three with lung cancer (1.2%), seven with prostatitis (2.7%), and one patient each (0.4% each) with hepatitis B, congestive heart failure, dementia, yaws, stroke, neoplastic disease, and depression with psychosis.

### Treatment outcomes in TB patients with co-morbidities

Overall treatment outcomes for the cohort (_N_ = 258) are summarized in Table2. Among the 258 TB patients with co-morbidities, 57.8% (_n_ = 149) achieved successful treatment outcomes. Specifically, 25.2% (_n_ = 65) completed treatment without confirmed bacteriological cure, while 32.6% (_n_ = 84) were cured based on bacteriological criteria. The remaining 42.2% had unfavourable outcomes: 33 patients (12.8%) defaulted (were lost to follow-up), 65 patients (25.2%) died during treatment, 10 (3.9%) had their treatment stopped by clinicians (usually due to severe adverse events or clinical deterioration), and 1 patient (0.4%) experienced treatment failure (persistent TB despite therapy).

### Treatment outcomes by specific co-morbidities

These notable patterns were observed in Table3: Only 56.4% patients with TB/HIV co-infection were treated successfully, and a considerable 28.2% died. They accounted for most deaths in the cohort (53 of 65 total deaths were in TB/HIV patients). The default rate among TB/HIV patients was 12.2%. TB patients with diabetes had the highest treatment success proportion (81.8% cured) and absence of observed adverse outcome. Patients with TB/hypertension outcomes were intermediate: 66.7% cured, 13.3% defaulted, 13.3% died. The TB patients with substance abuse fared poorly. They had the lowest treatment success rate (40%) and the highest mortality (33.3%) of any subgroup. Additionally, 4 patients (26.7%) defaulted, which is over twice the overall default rate. TB with other co-morbidities group had: 62.1% cured, 17.2% died, 13.8% defaulted. The deaths in this group included patients with severe conditions (e.g. 2 with cancer, 1 with stroke complications). The default cases in this group did not show a clear pattern by specific condition. Mortality was recorded as all-cause mortality during TB treatment, without adjudication of TB-specific causes.

### Association between co-morbidity and treatment outcome

A chi-square test (considering the five co-morbidity groups and three main outcome categories: cure, default, death) did not show a significant association between co-morbidity type and outcome (χ² = 5.40, df = 8, _p_ = 0.25). This suggests that, when taken as a whole, no specific co-morbidity category had a dramatically different outcome profile at the 5% significance level as shown in Table4; Fig.2. However, given some of the extreme proportions observed (especially for substance abuse and diabetes), specific comparisons were probed with 2 × 2 analyses:

### HIV vs. non-HIV

TB/HIV patients had a mortality of 28.2% compared to 17.1% among TB patients with other co-morbidities (12 deaths out of 70 non-HIV co-morbid patients). This yielded an unadjusted OR of ~ 1.90 for the odds of death in TB/HIV versus others, but this did not quite reach conventional significance (Fisher’s exact _p_ = 0.077, 95% CI for OR: 0.94–3.81). The trend indicates higher mortality with HIV, consistent with global evidence that TB/HIV co-infection increases risk of death. For treatment default, the difference was smaller: 12.2% default in HIV patient’s vs. 14.3% in non-HIV, OR ~ 0.84 (_p_ = 0.68), suggesting HIV by itself did not significantly increase default risk in this cohort.

### Substance abuse vs. others

Patients with substance abuse had over twice the default rate of other patients (26.7% vs. 11.3%). Although with 15 patients this difference did not reach statistical significance (OR ~ 2.68, _p_ = 0.11), it is clinically meaningful. The mortality difference (33.3% vs. 24.7% in others) was also notable but not significant (_p_ = 0.54). These comparisons are limited by the small sample, but they align with the expectation that substance abuse worsens adherence and outcomes.

### Diabetes vs. others

The diabetes group had 0% mortality vs. 26.3% among others. Fisher’s test yielded _p_ = 0.07 for the difference (borderline significant). Although numbers are few, it appears the diabetic TB patients did unexpectedly well. It is possible that diabetic patients in this setting received more intensive monitoring or had less advanced TB (or that those with very poor prognosis died before or shortly after TB diagnosis and were not captured).

### Hypertension vs. others

The outcome differences for hypertensive TB patients were minor. Default and death rates (~ 13% each) were like those without hypertension. Thus, hypertension (when controlled) might not significantly affect short-term TB outcomes, though chronic cardiovascular disease could influence long-term survival beyond TB treatment.

### Factors influencing treatment default

Out of 258 patients, 33 defaulted (12.8%). Specifically, 27 of the 33 defaulters (81.8%) were aged 15–34 years. The age distribution of defaulters was: 3 (9.1%) in age 15–24, 24 (72.7%) in 25–34, 4 (12.1%) in 35–44, and only 2 (6.1%) in 45–54, with none above 54. In contrast, among patients who completed treatment (successfully or not), only 16.7% were under 35. Thus, younger patients were far more likely to default. When dichotomized at 35 years: 36.0% of patients < 35 years defaulted vs. only 3.3% of those ≥ 35. This difference was highly significant (χ² test, _p_< 0.001). The estimated OR was 16.6 (95% CI ~ 6.4–43.4) for default if < 35 vs. older, underscoring that younger age was a strong risk factor for default in this study. This is consistent with national data showing higher default rates in younger TB patients [4].

Marital status also showed a clear association. Among the 33 defaulters, 22 (66.7%) were single and 10 (30.3%) were married, with 1 (3%) cohabiting. In contrast, in the overall cohort single individuals were 28.3%. Thus, singles were over-represented among defaulters. It was found that 30.1% of single patients defaulted vs. only 5.9% of those who were married or living with a partner. This difference was statistically significant (Fisher’s exact _p_< 0.001; OR = 6.8, 95% CI 2.9–15.9). Not having a spouse or treatment supporter at home might contribute to non-adherence, as also reflected in patient-reported reasons.

By sex, there was a slight trend of more male defaulters (21 males vs. 12 females defaulted, 13.5% of all males’ vs. 11.8% of all females), but this was not significant (_p_ = 0.70). It appears that, sex was less important than age and marital status in determining default, even though globally males often default slightly more.

There was no strong direct relationship between specific co-morbidities and default in univariate analysis (aside from the substance abuse trend noted). This was expected given the dominant role of age and social factors. In the multivariate logistic regression, only younger age and single marital status remained independently associated with higher odds of default, while co-morbidity variables did not. This reinforces that demographic and social factors were the primary drivers of default in this study.

### Default profile

In terms of default profile, 22 of 33 defaulters (66.7%) were single, and 81.8% were aged < 35, as noted. Additionally, 78.8% of defaulters were pulmonary TB cases (only 7 of the 33 had extrapulmonary TB), indicating perhaps that most EPTB patients were managed with more intensive follow-up (and many EPTB cases were co-managed with surgical or other departments, possibly influencing adherence). Co-morbidity-wise, defaulters included: 23 were HIV-positive (12.2% of all TB/HIV patients), 4 had substance abuse (26.7% of substance users defaulted), 2 had hypertension (13.3% of hypertensives defaulted), and 4 had other conditions; notably, none of the 11 diabetic patients defaulted.

## Discussion

### Prevalence of co-morbidities

This study set out to evaluate how co-morbid conditions influence TB treatment outcomes at a leading chest clinic in Ghana. It was found that co-morbidities are extremely common among TB patients in this tertiary setting – about one in four TB cases over 2021–2022 had at least one significant co-morbidity, with HIV being the most prevalent. The high TB/HIV co-infection rate (72.9% in this co-morbid subset) underscores the heavy overlap of the two epidemics in urban Ghana. While this percentage is not reflective of all TB patients (it is much higher than the ~ 18% co-infection rate in the general TB population of Ghana [4]), it highlights that HIV remains the dominant co-morbidity among those TB patients who require tertiary care. This aligns with global patterns [14]. The practice of routine HIV screening (over 94% of TB cases tested) is commendable and in line with WHO recommendations, contributing to early identification and management of co-infected patients.

### Treatment outcome and co-morbidity

The impact of co-morbidities on outcomes was evident in the overall treatment success rate of only 57.8%, which is far below the national target (≥ 85%). This suggests that co-morbid TB patients experience substantially worse outcomes than TB patients without co-morbidities. Indeed, co-morbidities like HIV and substance abuse can complicate TB treatment through immune suppression, drug interactions, and poor adherence [15]. The stark outcome that 25.2% patients died during therapy indicate the high severity of illness in this group.

By comparison, none of the 11 TB/diabetes patients died, with success rate of 82%. This finding is counterintuitive given global evidence that diabetes typically worsens TB outcomes. One hypothesis is that the TB/DM patients might have benefited from integrated care or closer monitoring (e.g., blood glucose control during TB therapy), mitigating the risks. Alternatively, the diabetic patients may have had less advanced TB disease or other favourable characteristics (they tended to be older and perhaps more adherent). Regardless, the data suggest that with proper management, TB/diabetes co-infection can be effectively handled – though the sample was small.

### Default predictors

The analysis of default predictors revealed that age and marital status were the key factors. Patients under 35 had enormously higher odds of defaulting treatment, and being single was another strong predictor. These social/demographic factors overshadowed medical factors in predicting non-adherence. This resonates with programmatic observations: younger patients often have more mobility (travel for work or school), may lack stable support systems, and sometimes have risk-taking behaviours, all of which can lead to treatment interruption. Similarly, single patients might lack the family support or accountability that encourages adherence. The findings in this regard mirror those from other settings – for instance, studies in Rwanda and Pakistan have identified youth and lack of family support as risk factors for default [16, 17]. Interestingly, the study did not find male sex to be a significant factor in default (males and females defaulted at roughly similar rates in this cohort), even though some literature notes males can have slightly higher default rates. Being young and single trumped gender as risk factors, possibly because these characteristics cut across both males and females.

The outcome of this research suggested that substance abuse co-morbidity was associated with a notably high default rate (26.7%) and the lowest treatment success rate (40%). Although the sample size for this subgroup was small (_n_ = 15), the trend is worrying and consistent with reports from other countries that substance use impairs TB treatment adherence and outcomes. Alcohol abuse can cause patients to miss doses and appointments due to intoxication or social instability, and it can exacerbate side effects and toxicity of TB medications. While the study did not have enough power to conclusively quantify the effect (_p_ = 0.11 for higher default in substance users), the qualitative and trend data emphasize the need for targeted interventions in this group (e.g., counselling, addiction support, enlisting treatment supporters). This aligns with other studies linking substance abuse to higher default and failure rates in TB care [10, 11].

In contrast, HIV co-infection, despite its very high prevalence, was not a significant predictor of default– TB/HIV patients defaulted at about the same rate as others. This suggests that the clinic’s adherence support for TB/HIV patients might have been effective, or that HIV status by itself does not determine adherence as much as social factors do. However, HIV had a major impact on mortality: over 28% of TB/HIV patients died, which accounted for most deaths in the study. This outcome underscores the severity of TB/HIV co-morbidity, consistent with systematic reviews showing much higher TB mortality in HIV-positive patients [5].

These findings echo calls to integrate non-communicable disease management with TB care [18]. As chronic diseases like diabetes rise in TB-endemic regions, adopting lessons from TB/HIV integration could improve outcomes [19].

Although hypertension is not traditionally classified among the major immunosuppressive comorbidities like HIV or diabetes mellitus, emerging evidence suggests that it may influence TB pathophysiology and treatment outcomes through several indirect mechanisms. Chronic hypertension is associated with systemic low-grade inflammation and elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF-α, which may dysregulate the host immune response required to control _Mycobacterium tuberculosis_ infection [20].

Moreover, TB patients with hypertension often manage multiple chronic conditions concurrently, leading to increased pill burden and a higher risk of non-adherence to TB therapy. This may compromise treatment efficacy and result in unfavourable outcomes [13]. Additionally, anti-TB medications such as rifampicin and isoniazid are hepatotoxic and nephrotoxic, and in patients with existing cardiovascular or renal compromise due to hypertension, the risk of adverse drug reactions may be amplified [21].

These mechanisms suggest that even though hypertension was not a statistically significant predictor in our model, its presence in TB patients warrants clinical attention and integrated care planning.

This study has limitations that must be acknowledged when interpreting the results. The design was retrospective and observational, relying on routine clinical records. As a result, some data were missing or not recorded in detail. For example, there was no data on CD4 counts, HIV viral loads, or precise measures of alcohol consumption. The study was conducted at a single tertiary hospital’s chest clinic, which may limit generalizability. Sample size limitations affected some analyses. The number of patients in certain subgroups was small (e.g., only 11 with diabetes, 15 with substance abuse). This reduces the statistical power to detect differences and yields wide confidence intervals. Despite these limitations, the study provides useful insights. The limitations mainly suggest that the quantitative effect estimates should be interpreted with caution and in context, and that further research (preferably prospective and multi-centre) is warranted to build on these findings. The results of this study have been triangulated with existing evidence to bolster credibility where possible. The recommendations provided consider both the findings and their limitations, aiming to improve care for TB patients with co-morbidities.

## Conclusions

In this cross-sectional study of TB patients with co-morbidities at a major Ghanaian teaching hospital, co-morbid conditions significantly influence treatment outcomes and pose challenges to TB control. HIV was the most common co-morbidity, affecting 72.9% of co-morbid TB patients, followed by substance abuse and hypertension (each 5.8%). Even though HIV-associated TB was most prevalent, TB patients with substance abuse issues experienced the worst outcomes. In contrast, TB patients with diabetes had an 82% treatment success rate and no recorded deaths, suggesting that with integrated care, TB/diabetes co-infection can be effectively managed, although this finding must be viewed cautiously due to the small sample.

Overall, the findings confirm that co-morbidities are associated with higher risks of poor outcomes (death or default), even if not all differences were statistically significant. Importantly, younger and single patients were disproportionately likely to default on treatment.

These findings underscore the need for integrated care strategies that address both TB and co-existing chronic diseases. Strengthening the management of co-morbid illnesses alongside TB treatment may improve patient outcomes and boost overall treatment success rates.

## Abstract

### Background

In Ghana, tuberculosis (TB) cases reached 19,000 in 2023 (15% above 2022). Co-morbidities such as human immunodeficient virus (HIV), diabetes, substance abuse, and hypertension can complicate treatment. The study evaluated co-morbidity prevalence among TB patients at a major Ghanaian hospital and their impact on treatment outcomes (treatment success, default, death).

### Methods

A retrospective descriptive cross-sectional study at the Chest Clinic, Korle-Bu Teaching Hospital, Accra, reviewed 2021–2022 records of 993 TB patients of which 258 had ≥ 1 co-morbidity. Demographics, co-morbidities (HIV, diabetes, substance abuse, hypertension), and outcomes (cure, default, death) were recorded. Associations between co-morbidities and outcomes were analysed using chi-square tests and logistic regression.

### Results

Of the 993 TB patients, 258/993 (26.0%) had TB with comorbidity and 149/258 (57.8%) were treated successfully. The 258 comorbid TB patients (mean age 44 ± 15 years) were 60.5% male and 53.9% married with co-morbidities: HIV 72.9%, hypertension 5.8%, substance abuse 5.8% and diabetes 4.3%. The TB/HIV patients had 28.2% mortality and substance abusers had 33.3% mortality. Higher odds of death were seen in TB/HIV (OR ≈ 1.90, 95% CI 0.94–3.81, _p_ = 0.08) and substance abuse (OR ≈ 1.53, _p_ = 0.54). TB/diabetes showed a non-significant survival benefit (0% vs. ~ 26% in others, _p_ = 0.07). Default was 12.8% overall and it was higher in substance abusers (26.7% vs. 13.2%, OR ≈ 2.68, 95% CI 0.82–8.8, _p_ = 0.11). Younger age and single status strongly predicted default: <35 vs. ≥ 35 years (36.0% vs. 3.3%, OR = 16.6, 95% CI 6.4–43.4, _p_< 0.001); single vs. partnered (30.1% vs. 5.9%, OR = 6.8, 95% CI 2.9–15.9, _p_< 0.001). However, findings may not be generalizable to rural or primary care settings, which is acknowledged as a study limitation.

### Conclusions

TB patients with co-morbid conditions experienced poorer treatment outcomes than patients without such co-morbidities. These findings underscore the need for integrated care strategies that address both TB and co-existing chronic diseases. Strengthening the management of co-morbid illnesses alongside TB treatment may improve patient outcomes and boost overall treatment success rates.

## Background

Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major global health threat, causing an estimated 10.8 million new cases and 1.25 million deaths in 2023. It has re-emerged as the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent, surpassing even COVID-19 [1]. The burden of TB is heaviest in low- and middle-income countries with fragile health systems, especially in sub-Saharan Africa. In 2022, Africa accounted for about 2.5 million new TB cases and 424,000 TB-related deaths, representing over one-third of global TB deaths [2]. Ghana has experienced a worrying rise in TB cases; for example, 19,000 cases were recorded in 2023 though the World Health Organisation (WHO) projections is showing decreasing TB incidence in Ghana (130 per 100,000 in 2024) [1]. TB in Ghana continues to be a significant cause of morbidity and mortality, responsible for over 5% of all deaths annually in the country [3].

National TB program data show that from 2018 to 2022, Ghana recorded fluctuating TB treatment success rates between 78% and 88%, slightly below the global average of 88% in 2024 (WHO Global TB Report 2024). The case detection rate improved marginally from 36% in 2018 to 47% in 2022, yet this still falls short of the WHO target of 70% detection. TB mortality also remains high, with deaths often associated with delayed diagnosis, treatment default, and co-morbidities such as HIV/AIDS and diabetes mellitus [4].

HIV co-infection significantly complicates TB management in Ghana. Nationally, around 20% of TB patients are estimated to be HIV-positive, and this subgroup experiences poorer treatment outcomes. Diabetes mellitus, although less frequently reported, is increasingly recognized as a risk factor for adverse TB outcomes due to its immunosuppressive effects and potential interactions with TB medication [4].

Co-morbidities such as HIV/AIDS, diabetes mellitus (DM), substance abuse (alcohol or illicit drugs), hypertension and other chronic conditions pose additional challenges to TB control. These co-morbid conditions can worsen the course of TB and impede treatment success. HIV-infected individuals have a higher risk of developing active TB – an estimated 16–27 times higher than HIV-negative individuals [5] Global analyses indicate that TB treatment mortality in co-infected patients ranges from ~ 16% to 35%, compared to ~ 4–9% in TB patients without HIV [6].

Diabetes mellitus is another growing driver of adverse TB outcomes, given the increasing prevalence of type 2 diabetes in high-TB-burden countries. Diabetic patients have roughly a 3-fold higher risk of developing TB than non-diabetics, and diabetes can worsen TB disease severity and outcomes [7]. A systematic review reported that diabetes was associated with an ~ 1.9-fold increase in the risk of death during TB treatment and nearly 5-fold higher risk when controlling for other factors [7]. Biological mechanisms for this include diabetes-related immune dysfunction and possible pharmacokinetic interactions of TB drugs with hyperglycaemia or diabe8ic comorbidities. In Ghana, like many African countries, faces a rising diabetes prevalence alongside endemic TB, potentially creating a “double burden” that threatens TB control efforts [8].

Behavioural and substance use factors, such as alcohol abuse and smoking, are well-known to negatively influence TB treatment adherence and outcomes. Chronic alcohol use is associated with poor medication adherence, higher default rates, and liver toxicity on TB therapy [9]. Patients with alcohol use disorder have been found to be significantly more likely to default from TB treatment [10, 11]. Alcoholism and drug abuse also exacerbate poverty and reduce healthcare access, leading to delays in seeking care and increased loss to follow-up. A recent large cohort study in Europe found that alcoholism increased the odds of TB-related death by over eight-fold (OR 8.3) and substantially raised the risk of treatment failure [12].

Hypertension may not directly influence _Mycobacterium tuberculosis_ pathogenesis in the same way as diabetes or HIV, but its presence can indirectly affect TB outcomes through immune modulation, drug interactions, and comorbid cardiovascular risks [13].

In Ghana, several health system challenges continue to hinder effective TB diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up, particularly in rural and underserved regions. One critical issue is the shortage of skilled health personnel in rural areas, where TB patients often face delays in diagnosis and initiation of treatment due to the absence of trained clinicians and diagnostic infrastructure. Additionally, the supply chain for TB medications and diagnostic tools remains fragile, with frequent reports of stockouts and logistical bottlenecks that disrupt continuity of care. These supply chain inefficiencies affect not only first-line drugs but also laboratory reagents essential for bacteriological confirmation and follow-up testing [4].

Moreover, primary care facilities—where most TB cases are first encountered—are chronically underfunded, lacking both infrastructure and capacity to manage complex TB cases, particularly those involving co-morbid conditions like HIV and diabetes. This often results in late referrals to tertiary institutions, by which time patients may already be experiencing complications or advanced disease. Poor integration of TB services into the broader health system, limited community-based follow-up mechanisms, and inadequate patient tracking contribute further to loss to follow-up and poor treatment adherence. Addressing these systemic barriers is essential for improving TB outcomes and meeting national and global targets [1, 4].

Previous research in Ghana has reported TB/HIV co-infection rates around 11–23% in various regions, and treatment success rates nationally have remained suboptimal (approximately 85% in 2020) [4] amid challenges of drug-resistant TB and patients defaulting treatment).

However, there is limited data on how other co-morbidities (e.g. diabetes, hypertension, substance use) affect TB outcomes in the Ghanaian context, and which patient subgroups are at greatest risk of unfavourable outcomes (like treatment default or death).

The study was conducted at the Chest Clinic of the Korle-Bu Teaching Hospital (KBTH), Ghana’s largest national referral centre. Tertiary facilities often manage more complex TB cases, including patients with co-morbidities or advanced disease, making it an appropriate site for evaluating the impact of co-existing conditions on TB treatment outcomes. However, findings may not be generalizable to rural or primary care settings, which is acknowledged as a study limitation.

## Methods

### Study design and setting

This was a retrospective descriptive cross-sectional study conducted at the Chest Clinic of Korle-Bu Teaching Hospital (KBTH) in Accra, Ghana. KBTH is a large tertiary referral hospital that also serves as a national centre of excellence for chest diseases. The Chest Clinic provides outpatient and inpatient services for TB diagnosis and treatment, and it manages complicated TB cases referred from other parts of Ghana. The study targeted the period from January 2021 to December 2022, during which the hospital had fully implemented an electronic medical records system (Lightwave Health Information Management System, LHIMS) for TB patients. This timeframe was chosen to ensure data availability and completeness; TB case records before 2020 were less reliably captured electronically.

### Study population

The study population comprised all TB patients with at least one documented co-morbidity who registered for treatment at the Chest Clinic of KBTH between 2021 and 2022. According to clinic records, a total of 993 TB patients were managed in this period, out of which 258 had one or more co-morbid conditions recorded. The study included these 258 TB patients with co-morbidities in the analysis. Co-morbidity was defined as any additional diagnosed chronic condition alongside TB, such as HIV infection, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, substance use disorder (e.g. alcohol abuse), chronic liver disease, renal disease, malignancy, etc., as recorded in the patient’s medical notes. Both new TB cases and previously treated cases were included, provided they had a co-morbidity. Patients without any documented co-morbidity were excluded from this study.

### Data sources and collection

Data was extracted from the LHIMS electronic database and patient TB treatment cards. The parameters (TB, HIV, diabetes, hypertension, substance abuse etc.) were diagnosed using standard laboratory and clinical methods [1]. A standardized data abstraction form was used to collect relevant variables, including socio-demographic information (age, sex, marital status, level of education, employment status), clinical characteristics (type of TB – pulmonary vs. extrapulmonary, sputum smear/Xpert MTB status, HIV status, other co-morbidities), and] treatment outcomes. Co-morbidities were grouped into categories of interest (HIV, diabetes, hypertension (HTN), substance abuse, and others). “Substance abuse” predominantly referred to harmful alcohol use, as documented by clinic staff, but also included any illicit drug abuse if noted. The category “others” encompassed less common co-morbid conditions such as anaemia, malignancy, chronic malaria, chronic heart failure, chronic liver disease (including hepatitis B), mental health conditions, and other miscellaneous diagnoses (e.g., stroke, autoimmune disorders) that were each represented by only 1–2 cases.

The study recorded the specific outcomes of TB treatment as classified by the National Tuberculosis Control Program and WHO guidelines: Cured (completed treatment with documented bacteriological evidence of clearance, for sputum-positive cases), Treatment completed (completed therapy but without final sputum result); “Cured” and “completed” were combined as “successful treatment”; Defaulter (treatment interrupted for ≥ 2 consecutive months, now termed “Lost to Follow-up”), Died (death from any cause during treatment), and Treatment Failed (persistently positive sputum or clinically failed regimen). It was also noted if any patients had treatment stopped by clinicians due to severe adverse events or other reasons (this was recorded in a few cases). Additionally, for patients who defaulted, clinic records and outreach worker notes were reviewed to document the reasons for default as reported (e.g., lack of transport, adverse drug effects, etc.).

### Data analysis

Statistical analysis was performed using IBM SPSS (Version 26) and R (Version 4.3). Descriptive statistics were generated for all variables. Categorical variables (e.g. sex, co-morbidity type, treatment outcome category) were summarized as frequencies and percentages. Continuous variables like age were summarized by mean and standard deviation (SD) or median (interquartile range) as appropriate. The study population was stratified by co-morbidity categories and by key outcomes to facilitate comparisons.

The overall treatment outcome distributions (treatment success vs. defaulted vs. died vs. failed) was compared across the major co-morbidity groups (HIV, diabetes, hypertension, substance abuse, and other co-morbidities) using the chi-square test of independence. Given the small numbers in some outcome subcategories (e.g., only 1 treatment failure), the study focused on the three primary outcomes (cure, default, death) for comparison and considered “treatment failure” and “stopped” as rare events to mention qualitatively. Pairwise comparisons for specific outcomes of interest were conducted. Odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated for these comparisons, and Fisher’s exact test was used when cell counts were small. Tests with _p_< 0.05 were considered as statistically significant.

Additionally, predictors of treatment default were explored using logistic regression. The binary outcome was default (yes/no). The independent variables could influence adherence, specifically: age, sex, marital status, and presence of certain co-morbidities were included. Age was treated as a dichotomous variable (< 35 vs. ≥35 years) based on the observed association with default, and marital status was dichotomized as single vs. having a partner (married/cohabiting) for analysis. Given that no patients with diabetes defaulted, the diabetes variable in the regression model was not included to avoid complete separation issues. A backward stepwise approach was used to arrive at a parsimonious model. Adjusted odds ratios with 95% CI and p-values were reported for the final model covariates.

### Ethical considerations

The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Accra Technical University Research Ethics Committee with protocol identification number ATU/MLT/ET/003/2023–2024. As this was a retrospective record review, the need for informed consent from individual patients and consent for participation was waived by the Korle Bu Teaching Hospital Chest Clinic. All data were de-identified and kept confidential.

Every effort was made to ensure data accuracy and privacy. Only the research team had access to the raw data, which were stored on password-protected computers. In presenting results, the aggregate findings were reported without personal identifiers.

## Results

### Characteristics of the study population

A total of 258 TB patients (out of 933) with co-morbidities were included in the analysis as in Fig.1. The mean age was 44.3 years (SD ± 15.2), with a range from 15 to 85 years. The largest age group was 45–54 years (23.3% of patients), and 70.9% of patients were aged 25–54 (Table1). There was a male predominance: 156 (60.5%) were male and 102 (39.5%) were female, yielding a male: female ratio of ~ 1.5:1. Regarding marital status, 139 (53.9%) were married, 73 (28.3%) single, 28 (10.9%) divorced, 13 (5.0%) widowed, and 5 (1.9%) cohabiting. Most patients had some formal education – only 10% had no formal education, while 30% had secondary education and 23% had tertiary-level education. In terms of employment, 71% of patients were employed (formally or self-employed) and 10.5% were students. Pulmonary TB was the predominant form in this cohort; 201 patients (78.0%) had pulmonary TB, whereas 57 (22.1%) had extrapulmonary TB (lymphatic, pleural, spinal, or disseminated TB).

### Prevalence of co-morbidities

By design, all patients had at least one co-morbidity. Table1 shows the distribution of co-morbid conditions. HIV infection was the most prevalent co-morbidity, documented in 188 out of 258 patients, which is 72.9% of the study population (95% CI: 67.3%–78.0%). The next most common co-morbid conditions were hypertension and substance abuse; each found in 15 patients (5.8%). Substance abuse in medical records primarily referred to heavy alcohol use; a few cases also noted illicit drug use. Diabetes mellitus (mostly type 2) was present in 11 patients (4.3%). A variety of other co-morbidities were present at lower frequencies (collectively 11.2% when summed). These included four patients with anaemia (1.6%), three with chronic malaria (1.2%), three with lung cancer (1.2%), seven with prostatitis (2.7%), and one patient each (0.4% each) with hepatitis B, congestive heart failure, dementia, yaws, stroke, neoplastic disease, and depression with psychosis.

### Treatment outcomes in TB patients with co-morbidities

Overall treatment outcomes for the cohort (_N_ = 258) are summarized in Table2. Among the 258 TB patients with co-morbidities, 57.8% (_n_ = 149) achieved successful treatment outcomes. Specifically, 25.2% (_n_ = 65) completed treatment without confirmed bacteriological cure, while 32.6% (_n_ = 84) were cured based on bacteriological criteria. The remaining 42.2% had unfavourable outcomes: 33 patients (12.8%) defaulted (were lost to follow-up), 65 patients (25.2%) died during treatment, 10 (3.9%) had their treatment stopped by clinicians (usually due to severe adverse events or clinical deterioration), and 1 patient (0.4%) experienced treatment failure (persistent TB despite therapy).

### Treatment outcomes by specific co-morbidities

These notable patterns were observed in Table3: Only 56.4% patients with TB/HIV co-infection were treated successfully, and a considerable 28.2% died. They accounted for most deaths in the cohort (53 of 65 total deaths were in TB/HIV patients). The default rate among TB/HIV patients was 12.2%. TB patients with diabetes had the highest treatment success proportion (81.8% cured) and absence of observed adverse outcome. Patients with TB/hypertension outcomes were intermediate: 66.7% cured, 13.3% defaulted, 13.3% died. The TB patients with substance abuse fared poorly. They had the lowest treatment success rate (40%) and the highest mortality (33.3%) of any subgroup. Additionally, 4 patients (26.7%) defaulted, which is over twice the overall default rate. TB with other co-morbidities group had: 62.1% cured, 17.2% died, 13.8% defaulted. The deaths in this group included patients with severe conditions (e.g. 2 with cancer, 1 with stroke complications). The default cases in this group did not show a clear pattern by specific condition. Mortality was recorded as all-cause mortality during TB treatment, without adjudication of TB-specific causes.

### Association between co-morbidity and treatment outcome

A chi-square test (considering the five co-morbidity groups and three main outcome categories: cure, default, death) did not show a significant association between co-morbidity type and outcome (χ² = 5.40, df = 8, _p_ = 0.25). This suggests that, when taken as a whole, no specific co-morbidity category had a dramatically different outcome profile at the 5% significance level as shown in Table4; Fig.2. However, given some of the extreme proportions observed (especially for substance abuse and diabetes), specific comparisons were probed with 2 × 2 analyses:

### HIV vs. non-HIV

TB/HIV patients had a mortality of 28.2% compared to 17.1% among TB patients with other co-morbidities (12 deaths out of 70 non-HIV co-morbid patients). This yielded an unadjusted OR of ~ 1.90 for the odds of death in TB/HIV versus others, but this did not quite reach conventional significance (Fisher’s exact _p_ = 0.077, 95% CI for OR: 0.94–3.81). The trend indicates higher mortality with HIV, consistent with global evidence that TB/HIV co-infection increases risk of death. For treatment default, the difference was smaller: 12.2% default in HIV patient’s vs. 14.3% in non-HIV, OR ~ 0.84 (_p_ = 0.68), suggesting HIV by itself did not significantly increase default risk in this cohort.

### Substance abuse vs. others

Patients with substance abuse had over twice the default rate of other patients (26.7% vs. 11.3%). Although with 15 patients this difference did not reach statistical significance (OR ~ 2.68, _p_ = 0.11), it is clinically meaningful. The mortality difference (33.3% vs. 24.7% in others) was also notable but not significant (_p_ = 0.54). These comparisons are limited by the small sample, but they align with the expectation that substance abuse worsens adherence and outcomes.

### Diabetes vs. others

The diabetes group had 0% mortality vs. 26.3% among others. Fisher’s test yielded _p_ = 0.07 for the difference (borderline significant). Although numbers are few, it appears the diabetic TB patients did unexpectedly well. It is possible that diabetic patients in this setting received more intensive monitoring or had less advanced TB (or that those with very poor prognosis died before or shortly after TB diagnosis and were not captured).

### Hypertension vs. others

The outcome differences for hypertensive TB patients were minor. Default and death rates (~ 13% each) were like those without hypertension. Thus, hypertension (when controlled) might not significantly affect short-term TB outcomes, though chronic cardiovascular disease could influence long-term survival beyond TB treatment.

### Factors influencing treatment default

Out of 258 patients, 33 defaulted (12.8%). Specifically, 27 of the 33 defaulters (81.8%) were aged 15–34 years. The age distribution of defaulters was: 3 (9.1%) in age 15–24, 24 (72.7%) in 25–34, 4 (12.1%) in 35–44, and only 2 (6.1%) in 45–54, with none above 54. In contrast, among patients who completed treatment (successfully or not), only 16.7% were under 35. Thus, younger patients were far more likely to default. When dichotomized at 35 years: 36.0% of patients < 35 years defaulted vs. only 3.3% of those ≥ 35. This difference was highly significant (χ² test, _p_< 0.001). The estimated OR was 16.6 (95% CI ~ 6.4–43.4) for default if < 35 vs. older, underscoring that younger age was a strong risk factor for default in this study. This is consistent with national data showing higher default rates in younger TB patients [4].

Marital status also showed a clear association. Among the 33 defaulters, 22 (66.7%) were single and 10 (30.3%) were married, with 1 (3%) cohabiting. In contrast, in the overall cohort single individuals were 28.3%. Thus, singles were over-represented among defaulters. It was found that 30.1% of single patients defaulted vs. only 5.9% of those who were married or living with a partner. This difference was statistically significant (Fisher’s exact _p_< 0.001; OR = 6.8, 95% CI 2.9–15.9). Not having a spouse or treatment supporter at home might contribute to non-adherence, as also reflected in patient-reported reasons.

By sex, there was a slight trend of more male defaulters (21 males vs. 12 females defaulted, 13.5% of all males’ vs. 11.8% of all females), but this was not significant (_p_ = 0.70). It appears that, sex was less important than age and marital status in determining default, even though globally males often default slightly more.

There was no strong direct relationship between specific co-morbidities and default in univariate analysis (aside from the substance abuse trend noted). This was expected given the dominant role of age and social factors. In the multivariate logistic regression, only younger age and single marital status remained independently associated with higher odds of default, while co-morbidity variables did not. This reinforces that demographic and social factors were the primary drivers of default in this study.

### Default profile

In terms of default profile, 22 of 33 defaulters (66.7%) were single, and 81.8% were aged < 35, as noted. Additionally, 78.8% of defaulters were pulmonary TB cases (only 7 of the 33 had extrapulmonary TB), indicating perhaps that most EPTB patients were managed with more intensive follow-up (and many EPTB cases were co-managed with surgical or other departments, possibly influencing adherence). Co-morbidity-wise, defaulters included: 23 were HIV-positive (12.2% of all TB/HIV patients), 4 had substance abuse (26.7% of substance users defaulted), 2 had hypertension (13.3% of hypertensives defaulted), and 4 had other conditions; notably, none of the 11 diabetic patients defaulted.

## Discussion

### Prevalence of co-morbidities

This study set out to evaluate how co-morbid conditions influence TB treatment outcomes at a leading chest clinic in Ghana. It was found that co-morbidities are extremely common among TB patients in this tertiary setting – about one in four TB cases over 2021–2022 had at least one significant co-morbidity, with HIV being the most prevalent. The high TB/HIV co-infection rate (72.9% in this co-morbid subset) underscores the heavy overlap of the two epidemics in urban Ghana. While this percentage is not reflective of all TB patients (it is much higher than the ~ 18% co-infection rate in the general TB population of Ghana [4]), it highlights that HIV remains the dominant co-morbidity among those TB patients who require tertiary care. This aligns with global patterns [14]. The practice of routine HIV screening (over 94% of TB cases tested) is commendable and in line with WHO recommendations, contributing to early identification and management of co-infected patients.

### Treatment outcome and co-morbidity

The impact of co-morbidities on outcomes was evident in the overall treatment success rate of only 57.8%, which is far below the national target (≥ 85%). This suggests that co-morbid TB patients experience substantially worse outcomes than TB patients without co-morbidities. Indeed, co-morbidities like HIV and substance abuse can complicate TB treatment through immune suppression, drug interactions, and poor adherence [15]. The stark outcome that 25.2% patients died during therapy indicate the high severity of illness in this group.

By comparison, none of the 11 TB/diabetes patients died, with success rate of 82%. This finding is counterintuitive given global evidence that diabetes typically worsens TB outcomes. One hypothesis is that the TB/DM patients might have benefited from integrated care or closer monitoring (e.g., blood glucose control during TB therapy), mitigating the risks. Alternatively, the diabetic patients may have had less advanced TB disease or other favourable characteristics (they tended to be older and perhaps more adherent). Regardless, the data suggest that with proper management, TB/diabetes co-infection can be effectively handled – though the sample was small.

### Default predictors

The analysis of default predictors revealed that age and marital status were the key factors. Patients under 35 had enormously higher odds of defaulting treatment, and being single was another strong predictor. These social/demographic factors overshadowed medical factors in predicting non-adherence. This resonates with programmatic observations: younger patients often have more mobility (travel for work or school), may lack stable support systems, and sometimes have risk-taking behaviours, all of which can lead to treatment interruption. Similarly, single patients might lack the family support or accountability that encourages adherence. The findings in this regard mirror those from other settings – for instance, studies in Rwanda and Pakistan have identified youth and lack of family support as risk factors for default [16, 17]. Interestingly, the study did not find male sex to be a significant factor in default (males and females defaulted at roughly similar rates in this cohort), even though some literature notes males can have slightly higher default rates. Being young and single trumped gender as risk factors, possibly because these characteristics cut across both males and females.

The outcome of this research suggested that substance abuse co-morbidity was associated with a notably high default rate (26.7%) and the lowest treatment success rate (40%). Although the sample size for this subgroup was small (_n_ = 15), the trend is worrying and consistent with reports from other countries that substance use impairs TB treatment adherence and outcomes. Alcohol abuse can cause patients to miss doses and appointments due to intoxication or social instability, and it can exacerbate side effects and toxicity of TB medications. While the study did not have enough power to conclusively quantify the effect (_p_ = 0.11 for higher default in substance users), the qualitative and trend data emphasize the need for targeted interventions in this group (e.g., counselling, addiction support, enlisting treatment supporters). This aligns with other studies linking substance abuse to higher default and failure rates in TB care [10, 11].

In contrast, HIV co-infection, despite its very high prevalence, was not a significant predictor of default– TB/HIV patients defaulted at about the same rate as others. This suggests that the clinic’s adherence support for TB/HIV patients might have been effective, or that HIV status by itself does not determine adherence as much as social factors do. However, HIV had a major impact on mortality: over 28% of TB/HIV patients died, which accounted for most deaths in the study. This outcome underscores the severity of TB/HIV co-morbidity, consistent with systematic reviews showing much higher TB mortality in HIV-positive patients [5].

These findings echo calls to integrate non-communicable disease management with TB care [18]. As chronic diseases like diabetes rise in TB-endemic regions, adopting lessons from TB/HIV integration could improve outcomes [19].

Although hypertension is not traditionally classified among the major immunosuppressive comorbidities like HIV or diabetes mellitus, emerging evidence suggests that it may influence TB pathophysiology and treatment outcomes through several indirect mechanisms. Chronic hypertension is associated with systemic low-grade inflammation and elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF-α, which may dysregulate the host immune response required to control _Mycobacterium tuberculosis_ infection [20].

Moreover, TB patients with hypertension often manage multiple chronic conditions concurrently, leading to increased pill burden and a higher risk of non-adherence to TB therapy. This may compromise treatment efficacy and result in unfavourable outcomes [13]. Additionally, anti-TB medications such as rifampicin and isoniazid are hepatotoxic and nephrotoxic, and in patients with existing cardiovascular or renal compromise due to hypertension, the risk of adverse drug reactions may be amplified [21].

These mechanisms suggest that even though hypertension was not a statistically significant predictor in our model, its presence in TB patients warrants clinical attention and integrated care planning.

This study has limitations that must be acknowledged when interpreting the results. The design was retrospective and observational, relying on routine clinical records. As a result, some data were missing or not recorded in detail. For example, there was no data on CD4 counts, HIV viral loads, or precise measures of alcohol consumption. The study was conducted at a single tertiary hospital’s chest clinic, which may limit generalizability. Sample size limitations affected some analyses. The number of patients in certain subgroups was small (e.g., only 11 with diabetes, 15 with substance abuse). This reduces the statistical power to detect differences and yields wide confidence intervals. Despite these limitations, the study provides useful insights. The limitations mainly suggest that the quantitative effect estimates should be interpreted with caution and in context, and that further research (preferably prospective and multi-centre) is warranted to build on these findings. The results of this study have been triangulated with existing evidence to bolster credibility where possible. The recommendations provided consider both the findings and their limitations, aiming to improve care for TB patients with co-morbidities.

## Conclusions

In this cross-sectional study of TB patients with co-morbidities at a major Ghanaian teaching hospital, co-morbid conditions significantly influence treatment outcomes and pose challenges to TB control. HIV was the most common co-morbidity, affecting 72.9% of co-morbid TB patients, followed by substance abuse and hypertension (each 5.8%). Even though HIV-associated TB was most prevalent, TB patients with substance abuse issues experienced the worst outcomes. In contrast, TB patients with diabetes had an 82% treatment success rate and no recorded deaths, suggesting that with integrated care, TB/diabetes co-infection can be effectively managed, although this finding must be viewed cautiously due to the small sample.

Overall, the findings confirm that co-morbidities are associated with higher risks of poor outcomes (death or default), even if not all differences were statistically significant. Importantly, younger and single patients were disproportionately likely to default on treatment.

These findings underscore the need for integrated care strategies that address both TB and co-existing chronic diseases. Strengthening the management of co-morbid illnesses alongside TB treatment may improve patient outcomes and boost overall treatment success rates.

The double burden of tuberculosis (TB) and diabetes mellitus (DM) represents a major public health chal-

lenge that demands urgent and integrated approaches. The interplay between these two chronic condi-

tions presents unique clinical and public health management challenges, as well as social and economic 

implications. We explored the bidirectional relationship between TB and DM, emphasizing how DM in-

creases susceptibility to TB and complicates its management, while TB may exacerbate glycemic control 

in diabetic patients. This review underscores the challenges associated with the management of both 

diseases, obstacles in screening TB patients for DM and TB preventive therapy for DM since inadequate 

glycemic control can impact treatment outcomes. Several studies have investigated the disease interplay; 

however, the results have been equivocal, and this may be exerting negative impacts on the disease pre-

vention and treatment. TB-diabetes comorbidity has been linked to poor treatment outcomes whereas TB 

prevention in people with DM at present is a dilemma. In addition to highlighting how urgent it is to 

address this comorbidity, this review offers a road map for better prevention, treatment, and control of 

several factors underlying the TB-diabetes syndemic interaction.

Introduction 

The global burden of tuberculosis (TB) and diabetes melli-

tus (DM) is substantial, and these diseases disproportionately af-

fect the most vulnerable populations, including people living in 

poverty, malnourished individuals, and the aged. TB remains a sig-

nificant global health challenge despite sustained efforts to pre-

vent, detect, and treat the disease [1]. It is the 13th cause of death 

worldwide and the deadliest infectious disease after COVID-19, and 

experts predict that if not controlled, it will become the world’s 

number one cause of death [1,2]. The TB situation varies signifi-

cantly across different geographical regions [2]. The highest bur-

den of TB is borne by low- and middle-income countries [3], with 

around 87% of all cases reported in sub-Saharan Africa, Asia, and 

South America.

Additionally, there are pathogen derived risk factors including, 

the emergence of drug-resistant strains such as multidrug resis-

tant TB (MDR-TB) and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB), and 

the ability of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) to transition from 

latent to active TB disease. The pathogen associated risk factors 

can be aggravated by challenges in delivering effective treatment

Epidemiology: trends, and clinical presentation of TB-DM 

Mycobacterium tuberculosis is perhaps the most successful infec-

tious agent in current times. Despite its long history and numerous 

interventions put in place to address it, the incidence and preva-

lence of TB continues to increase. Each day, about 40 0 0 people lose 

their lives to TB and close to 28,0 0 0 people fall ill with this pre-

ventable and curable disease [1]. In 2022, the World Health Or-

ganization (WHO) estimated that 10.3 million people comprising 

of 8 million men, 3.5 million women and 1.3 million children fell 

ill with TB [2]. This represents a two-year reversal in the decline 

of the incidence of TB that was seen in the prior years and fur-

ther impedes the End TB goals. It is thus imperative to identify 

and study all factors that increase the risk of TB if the global goal 

of an 80% reduction in the incidence of TB and 90% reduction in 

deaths related to TB is to be achieved by 2030 [1]. 

Multiple studies have shown a strong association between DM 

and TB especially in low- and middle- income countries where TB 

is endemic, and the burden of DM is increasing [3-6 ]. About 95% 

of TB and 75% of the DM cases live in low- and middle-income 

countries [3,4,6]. In fact, of the ten countries with the highest 

number of DM patients worldwide, 6 are classified as “high bur-

den” for TB by the WHO, meaning they contribute to 80% of the 

TB cases worldwide [1]. The co-occurrence of TB-DM is not likely 

to decline anytime soon as DM weakens a person’s immune sys-

tem and increases the risk of getting active TB [5,6]. Similarly, TB 

causes “stress-induced hyperglycemia” and this can make the man-

agement of DM more difficult [3,5,6]. This is concerning as poor 

glycemic control has been linked to poor outcomes in TB treat-

ment. 

The global prevalence of TB-DM comorbidity ranges from 

13.73% [8] to 15.3% [7] varying from 0·1% in Latvia to 45 ·2% -

50.12% in Marshall Islands [7]. This wide variation in observations 

may be explained by the diverse nature of the diabetic popula-

tion [7,8]. Regionally, the prevalence of patients with DM and TB 

has been observed to be 19.32% in the Americas, 17.31% in Europe, 

14.62% in Southeast Asia, 13.59% in the western Pacific region, 

9.61% in the eastern Mediterranean region, and 9.30% in Africa [8]. 

The trend, as depicted from the studies spanning from 2014 to 

2024 (Table 1), indicates a steady increase in the disease preva-

lence among adults. The percentage of TB patients with DM var-

ied from 8.5% to 11% during 2016 to 2018 [9] and reaching as 

high as 45% [7,10 ], while patients in TB endemic countries like 

South Africa, Peru, Romania, and Indonesia was 12.5% according 

to a study that assessed DM status and clinical correlates in TB 

patients across these settings [11 ]. The prevalence of DM among 

TB patients in Sub-Saharan Africa was found to be 9.0% based 

on a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational stud-

ies [12 ]. This study included data from various countries in Sub-

Saharan Africa, with the highest prevalence reported in Nigeria at 

15%, followed by Tanzania at 11%, and Ethiopia at 10%. In Ghana, 

the prevalence was 9.4% among 2,990 TB patients enrolled in 2016 

[13 ]. The high prevalence of TB-DM comorbidity is linked to sev-

eral key factors, including urbanization, sedentary lifestyles, obe-

sity, population growth, and aging. These drivers are particularly 

significant in countries where TB is endemic. 

Longitudinal analysis of 163 studies reported increased TB inci-

dence in settings where DM prevalence increased over time [6]. A

systematic review of 13 observational cases globally revealed that 

DM was associated with a 3-fold increase in the incidence of pul-

monary TB (RR = 3.11, 95% CI 2.27-4.26) [5]. A South Asian study 

found that 11-24% of TB patients also have DM comorbidity, with 

variations across and within countries like India (14-25% preva-

lence) [10 ]. This increase in the risk of developing TB-DM is once 

again more evident in low- and middle-income countries [3,6,7]. 

However, even in countries with a low burden of TB, studies have 

shown that patients with DM have a higher risk of developing 

TB. DM is consistently linked to a higher risk of TB across various 

study designs and populations, with a relative risk of 3.11 and odds 

ratios ranging from 1.16 to 7.83, showing higher effect estimates in 

non-North American studies [5]. Noubiap et al. [7] highlighted a

notably higher prevalence of DM among TB patients in the North 

America and Caribbean, western Pacific, southeast Asia, and Mid-

dle East and North Africa regions compared to Africa, South and 

Central America, and Europe, as revealed in subgroup and meta-

regression analyses. In specific regions, the risk of TB associated 

with DM was found to be comparable to or even higher than that 

linked to HIV infection, underscoring the significant impact of DM 

on TB burden in those areas [3,9]. 

Clinically, DM, particularly poorly controlled DM, is associated 

with a more severe and contagious TB infection as compared to 

the general population. TB-DM is associated with an increased fre-

quency of pulmonary TB (in contrast to extra-pulmonary disease) 

as compared to other diseases that compromise the immune sys-

tem [14 ]. This may be due to a hyper-reactive cell-mediated im-

mune response to MTB in DM patients that may be sub-optimal for 

containing MTB growth within the lung, but effective for prevent-

ing its dissemination and reactivation elsewhere [15 ]. TB-DM is 

also associated with increased lung cavitations, positive direct spu-

tum smears at the time of diagnosis, fever, cough, hemoptysis, and 

false-negative tuberculin skin test results [14 ]. There is also some 

evidence that DM prolongs smear and culture positivity at the end 

of the intensive phase of the TB treatment [6,14 ]. DM is also asso-

ciated with an increased risk of treatment complications, relapse, 

and mortality [10 ,16 ]. Gautam, et al. [10 ] in a meta-analysis re-

ported that DM increases the risk of treatment failure (OR = 1.65;

of mortality compared to non-diabetic TB patients. Conversely, the
