CI: 0.60-0.96, p < 0.001) [17 ]. Likewise, another analysis involving 

24 observational studies from 15 different countries revealed that 

DM has a significant positive association with MDR-TB (OR = 1.97, 

95% CI = 1.58-2.45, I2 = 38.2%, P value for heterogeneity = 0.031) ir-

respective of country income level, type of DM, how TB or DM was 

diagnosed, and design of primary studies [18 ]. However, two inde-

pendent studies by Ragouraman, et al. [9] and Gautam, et al. [10 ], 

in 2021 found no evidence for an increased risk of TB recurrence 

with drug resistant strains among people with DM. This empha-

sizes the need for more research into the TB-DM population. 

Host immune mechanism of TB-DM 

Pulmonary TB infection is mainly established through inhala-

tion of droplets of bacilli from an individual with active pulmonary 

TB through coughing, sneezing, talking, singing etc. Upon inhala-

tion, the bacilli interact with the bronchial epithelial cells which 

leads to a crosstalk between the MTB and the innate immune sys-

tem of the host [19 ]. Alveolar macrophages are likely the first types 

of antigen presenting cells that encounter the pathogen among 

others such as dendritic cells. After the encounter of MTB with the 

macrophages, phagocytosis takes place which leads to the uptake 

of the bacilli into phagosomes which fuse with lysosomes to form 

the phagolysosomes [20 ]. The phagolysosome functions to destroy 

the bacilli through the acidification of MTB in the phagolysosome 

by the actions of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species [20 ]. In-

fected myeloid dendritic cells travel to lymph nodes and with the 

help of neutrophils transform into mature dendritic cells. The ma-

ture dendritic cells activate lymphocytes through antigen presenta-

tion and induce adaptive immune responses [19 ]. The T cells travel 

to the lungs targeting MTB infected macrophages through the re-

lease of interferon gamma (IFN-γ ) and cytotoxic T cell where they 

stimulate an effective bactericidal response [15 ]. 

Additionally, some of the bacilli that escaped this process may 

be eliminated through the activation of vitamin-D receptors, which 

leads to the release of cathelicidin, anti-microbial peptides (AMP), 

and β-defensins, key in primary bacterial lysis [20 ,21 ]. Persons 

with deficit functions in these proteins may develop active TB, 

with the bacilli transported via the blood or lymphatic system. 

However, TB patients with comorbid DM, characterized by hy-

perglycemia and insulin resistance, often exhibit compromised im-

mune responses, predisposing them to primary TB infection or re-

activation of latent TB [19 ,20 ]. One significant contributing fac-

tor is the dysfunction of macrophages in DM, linked to cyto-

plasmic dsDNA/AIM2-associated pyroptosis, disrupting inflamma-

tory cytokine secretion, phagocytosis, chemotaxis, and immune 

defenses, thereby promoting bacterial growth and dissemination 

within the host [15 ,19 ,20 ,21 ]. Other factors may be responsible for 

the risk of TB disease among DM patients including: (1) the high 

blood glucose induces M2 polarization of macrophages instead of 

the classical M1 [19 ,21 ]. M2 macrophages functions in the control 

of host inflammation and generally supports MTB growth through 

the expression of high levels of anti-inflammatory cytokines such 

as IL-4 and IL-10. This also weakens the phagocytic ability of the 

macrophages leading to the evasion of the immune system. (2) 

Studies have shown that hyperglycemia increases the count of neu-

trophils however, there is also reduced migration of neutrophils to 

infected sites due to glycated collagen resulting from receptor gly-

cation end product on neutrophils [15 ,21 ]. There is also generally 

reduced chemotaxis, defective phagocytosis and reduced bacterici-

dal ability [15 ,21 ]. (3) The frequency of dendritic cells is also re-

duced significantly [21 ]. This reduces phagocytosis as well as the 

stimulation of CD4 T cells hence there is an overall decreased 

adaptive response to MTB infection in DM patients. (4) The fre-

quencies of Th1 and Th17 have been shown to decrease in DM 

patients due to increased frequency of Th2 that secretes IL4 [21 ]. 

Th2 is known to function to antagonize the frequencies of Th1 and 

Th17 [15 ,21 ]. Moreover, the ratio of Th1 and Th2 cytokines which 

control the secretions with each other, has been found to be gen-

erally lower in DM [19 ]. Hyperglycemia also leads to inhibited se-

cretion of IFN-γ and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) reducing 

the bactericidal effect on MTB [15 ]. This shows there is a drive to-

wards anti-inflammatory leading to reduced CD4 and CD8 T cells 

at sources of infection. This reduces the host immune response to 

the pathogen [20 ]. 

Bi-directional relationship between tuberculosis and diabetes 

mellitus 

TB and DM are mutually influential, with each condition poten-

tially affecting each other’s occurrence, presentation via a variety 

of mechanisms. The two have been described as "syndemic" be-

cause of their high co-occurrence rates, particularly in low- and 

middle-income countries [3]. On one hand, DM-related alterations 

in the respiratory system, such as impaired mucociliary clearance 

and pulmonary microangiopathy, facilitate the establishment and 

dissemination of TB bacteria in the lungs [22 ]. More importantly, 

DM increases the risk of TB infection, disease progression and 

death [13 ,16 ]. While on the other hand, TB can cause glucose in-

tolerance, worsen glycemic control [23 ], and exacerbates diabetes 

progression [16 ]. Individuals with comorbid TB tend to have more 

difficult forms of TB such as neuro tuberculosis and multidrug-

resistant TB [16 ,17 ,18 ]. This syndemic interaction highlight the ne-

cessity for a comprehensive approach that addresses both condi-

tions simultaneously in clinical management and public health in-

terventions. 

Impact of diabetes mellitus on tuberculosis 

Diabetes Mellitus Affects the Occurrence of Tuberculosis 

Biologically, DM fosters a more favorable environment for the 

conversion of latent TB infections (LTBI) into active TB disease 

(Figure 1) [11 ,15 ]. The generally accepted theory is that DM 

presents with a weakened immune system, facilitating the progres-

sion of LTBI to active TB [15 ], as explained below. This association 

is particularly relevant in non-pregnant populations, where DM, 

along with HIV infection, increases the likelihood of developing ac-

tive TB from LTBI [15 ]. Research has shown a moderately increased 

risk of LTBI in patients with DM from high TB incidence areas, sug-

gesting the need for combined screening for LTBI with other risk 

factors and comorbidities to identify high-risk groups effectively. 

There are substantial research and policy gaps in the prevention 

of TB disease in people with DM and the management of patients 

with TB-diabetes, highlighting the need for strategies such as tar-

geted vaccination programs, LTBI screening, and preventive therapy 

among DM patients. 

Elevated glucose levels in hyperglycemia create an environment 

conducive to MTB growth [21 ], promoting TB development in dia-

betic patients by affecting immune responses and generating Ad-

vanced Glycation End products (AGE) and chronic inflammation, 

increasing susceptibility to pathogens [21 ,23 ]. This increased TB 

burden in DM patients is attributed to the availability of sugars 

like trehalose, pyruvate, and glycerol, enabling MTB to evade host 

metabolic defenses and establish a favorable niche for growth and 

replication [21 ].

DM is associated with reduced levels of essential cytokines 

crucial for controlling MTB growth, such as IFN-γ and TNF-α

[20 ,21 ,24 ]. Macrophages from diabetic individuals exhibit dimin-

ished secretion of inflammatory cytokines like IL-1 β and TNF-

## α. The co-occurrence of DM and TB is associated with height-

ened systemic levels of proinflammatory cytokines, including IL-

1β, IL-6, and IL-18, alongside anti-inflammatory cytokines like IL-

10 [24 ]. Prolonged exposure to high glucose sensitizes macrophage 

responses to cytokine stimuli while reducing their phagocytic ac-

tivity, possibly due to metabolic pathway alterations [21 ]. Impaired 

immune response and reduced killing of intracellular bacteria in 

DM patients potentially increase bacterial load, chronic inflamma-

tion, and facilitate bacterial dissemination and severe forms of TB, 

emphasizing the importance of understanding the immunological 

and biochemical basis of TB susceptibility in DM patients for de-

veloping rational strategies to alleviate the dual burden of these 

diseases. 

Also, the microvascular complications of DM, such as impaired 

blood flow and poor tissue oxygenation in nephropathic situa-

tions, create hypoxic conditions that favor MTB survival. Lastly, the 

chronic inflammation caused by DM (redox imbalance stress) ex-

acerbates lung damage caused by TB, promoting a favorable envi-

ronment for MTB growth and exacerbating disease severity. 

There is the need for more basic immunological and clinical 

studies to the underlying mechanism of increased susceptibility to 

progression from latent mycobacterial infection to disease as well 

as negative outcomes of TB treatment. Also of equal importance 

is pharmacological studies to investigate the interaction between 

antidiabetic medication and that of TB. These studies are crucial 

as they have the potential to offer understanding and explore new 

therapeutic options for managing individuals with co-morbidity. 

Impact of diabetes mellitus on tuberculosis treatment outcome 

DM can lead to late reporting of TB. The common symptoms 

shared between DM and TB, such as weight loss and fatigue [23 ], 

can make TB undetected for longer periods, leading to delays in TB 

diagnosis and treatment initiation. 

Similarly, diabetic individuals may present with atypical radio-

logical findings as compared with TB patients without DM [14 ,23 ]. 

Diabetics typically experience abnormal radiographic patterns like 

miliary TB, lower lobe infiltrates, cavitation in the middle and up-

per lung zones, pleural effusion, and pulmonary nodules with cen-

tral low attenuation. When managing diabetics who are also TB 

coinfected, it is essential to recognize these unusual radiological 

abnormalities to make an accurate diagnosis and arrange an effi-

cient course of therapy. 

The coexistence of DM and TB can lead to decreased drug ab-

sorption (pined to altered gut motility, and impaired intestinal per-

meability), altered metabolism of anti-TB drugs, and reduced host 

response to treatment. Diabetes-related neuropathy often affects 

the enteric nervous system, leading to compromised gut motility 

and subsequent delayed drug absorption. Moreover, hyperglycemia 

in DM can alter gut permeability through the disruption of tight 

junction proteins [22 ]. This disrupted integrity allows for increased 

penetration of the MTB pathogens and hinders adequate absorp-

tion of the TB medications. 

Thus, individuals with DM have been reported to be more 

prone to treatment failure, relapse, and drug resistance [13 ,16 ,

17 ,18 ]. 

Compromised liver function resulting from both DM and TB fur-

ther exacerbates drug metabolism issues. Rifampin, a key anti-TB 

drug, can induce liver enzyme-cytochrome P450 and transporters-

P glycoproteins that metabolize oral anti-diabetic agents [25 ], and 

subsequently reduce the therapeutic concentrations and efficacies. 

This further leads to hyperglycemia which further worsens TB thus 

creating a vicious cycle. As a result, individuals with DM may have 

a slower response to anti-TB drugs and a higher risk of treatment 

failure or relapse. One study suggested that individuals with DM 

may require a longer duration of TB treatment to achieve success-

ful outcomes [9], contributing to increased healthcare costs and 

patient burden. 

Individuals with DM may be susceptible to hepatotoxicity, a

potential side effect of isoniazid and rifampin [26 ]. Diabetics are 

more prone to this because of the pre-existing liver involvement 

or compromised metabolic pathways with the use of both medica-

tions [26 ]. Lastly, the comorbidity of DM and TB can lead to higher 

mortality rates compared to either disease alone. This is attributed 

to the synergistic impact of impaired immune response, delayed 

diagnosis, increased treatment complications, and overall compro-

mised health. 

Effects of tuberculosis on diabetes mellitus 

The link between TB and DM was demonstrated in research 

where about 42.6% of active TB patients were reported to have im-

paired glucose tolerance that resolved following TB therapy [27 ]. 

Even though this hyperglycemia is transient, it can complicate the 

diagnosis of DM in TB patients. Patients may either be misdi-

agnosed with DM and thus may be exposed to the side effects 

of anti glycemic agents. In addition, failure to perform follow-up 

DM testing may miss individuals whose insulin resistance may 

worsen following TB treatment. TB can also lead to the develop-

ment of diabetes in several ways. First, hematological spread of 

bacilli from the primary pulmonary TB site can cause direct inva-

sion to other organs, for example, pancreas. The inflammatory re-

sponse mounted against TB can damage pancreatic beta cells, fur-

ther hampering insulin secretion and aggravating glucose home-

ostasis [28 ]. The radiological features resemble pancreatic malig-

nancy or pancreatitis [28 ], which in each case impair the correct 

function of the pancreas, that is, the production of insulin for the 

regulation of excess blood sugar. In all circumstances, the pancreas 

fails to release enough insulin, which causes blood sugar to build 

up and ultimately induce DM. 

Also, long standing TB infections often lead to chronic inflam-

mation, which can induce metabolic stress that may lead to the 

release of cortisol [29 ,30 ], a stress hormone produced in response 

to infection and chronic diseases. Cortisol suppresses the activity 

of T-cells, which are vital in controlling infections. Both TB and 

DM activate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, which 

may lead to increased cortisol production [30 ]. Chronically elevated 

cortisol levels exacerbate insulin resistance and impair glucose 

metabolism in individuals with DM [29 ,30 ], worsening glycemic 

control. This prolonged exposure to high cortisol levels weakens 

the immune system’s ability to fight infections, making individ-

uals more susceptible to TB infection and impairing their abil-

ity to clear the TB bacilli. This metabolic stress induced by cor-

tisol contributes to the reactivation of latent TB, further compro-

mising the health outcomes of affected individuals. Further de-

velopment of DM leads to compromises in the immune system 

stability and the cycle continues over and over as modeled in 

experiment. 

Challenges associated with the management of TB-DM Comorbid 

Individuals 

TB and DM can be treated simultaneously. Treating both condi-

tions concurrently is vital to ensure optimal outcomes for these pa-

tients, as untreated diabetes can compromise the immune system 

and effectiveness of TB treatment. Controlling blood glucose levels 

in patients with DM is essential to enhance optimal TB treatment 

[16 ,21 ,23 ]. In addition to lifestyle modifications, DM is managed by 

hypoglycemic agents such as metformin, sulfonylureas, DPP-4 in-

hibitors insulin therapy. Treating TB promptly with appropriate an-

tibiotics is crucial in preventing the worsening of diabetes control. 

However, treating patients with both TB and DM can prove to be 

complex and challenging due to the intricate relationship between 

these two diseases and some of the medications involved. The con-

ventional treatment regimen for drug susceptible new TB cases is 

isoniazid (H), rifampin (R), pyrazinamide (Z), and ethambutol (E) 

taken over a period of 6 months, taken under supervision. This ap-

proach, known as directly observed therapy short-course (DOTS), 

has proven to be effective in curing the disease. 

The possibility of drug-drug interactions between these two 

medications is one of the main difficulties. Most of the interactions 

are related to induction of cytochrome enzymes, which may lead 

to reduction in either the anti-diabetic agents or the anti-TB drugs, 

compromising their effectiveness and worsening the treatment 

outcomes in such individuals. Anti-TB medications like rifampin 

have the potential to induce liver enzymes [14 ], which could speed 

up the metabolism of diabetic medications and diminish their 

effectiveness [25 ]. Rifam picin through enzyme induction acceler-

ates the metabolism of sulfonylurea and biguanides reducing their 

plasma levels and thus leading to poor glucose control. Isoniazid 

may also antagonize the effect of sulfonylureas, also worsening 

glucose control. These drugs however do have an effect on the 

metabolism of insulin and as such the patients with active TB in-

fection may be forced to switch to using insulin despite its higher 

cost. Moreover, isoniazid and rifampin, the 2 key medications for 

sterilization against the MTB are known to be potent inducers 

and transporters of several anti-diabetic agents [25 ,26 ]. Rifampin 

is known to induce uridinediphosphate-glucuronosyl-transferases 

as well as influx and efflux important transporters including P-

glycoprotein in the liver, kidney, and erythrocytic cells that can af-

fect the metabolism of many medications including sulfonylureas, 

HIV protease inhibitors, and HIV nonnucleoside reverse transcrip-

tase inhibitors [25 ,26 ]. 

Anti-DM medications can also influence availability of anti-TB 

medications. The sulfonylureas and isoniazid are both metabolized 

in the liver by CYP2C9, so co-administration could increase isoni-

azid concentration levels in blood circulation. Due to this, sulfony-

lureas are discouraged in patients receiving anti-TB therapy [26 ]. 

Interestingly, metformin bypasses hepatic metabolism. Instead, it is 

absorbed by members of the solute carrier family via the organic 

cation transporter subtype 1 (OCT1) and eliminated unchanged by 

OCT2 in the kidneys. This unique pathway leads to minimal inter-

actions with anti-TB medications [31 ]. 

Metformin has a lesser effect on cytochrome P450 enzyme-

induced metabolism. In addition, it has been demonstrated to 

shorten the duration of TB treatment [23 ,31 ]. Metformin-exposed 

macrophages exhibited higher bactericidal activity because of in-

creased production of reactive oxidative species (ROS) required to 

eliminate bacteria in the mitochondria [31 ]. 

Only limited studies have been conducted to explore the cure 

rates of patients with both TB and DM, leaving the issue largely 

unexplored. Several studies that investigated the cure rates of TB 

patients with DM reveal a wide range of outcomes [16 ,17 ,32 ]. One 

research indicates that these patients have relatively lower cure 

rates compared to individuals without DM [32 ]. Factors contribut-

ing to this disparity include altered immune responses, altered gut 

motility and drug metabolism due to diabetes complications, and 

increased severity of TB symptoms, due to suboptimal glucose con-

trol.

A significant additional challenge is the increased likelihood of 

adverse effects and treatment challenges brought on by the con-

comitant use of both medications. When administered together, 

the side effects of TB and DM medications frequently overlap. Pa-

tients taking anti-TB drugs run the risk of developing drug-induced 

neuropathies, hepatotoxicity, or digestive issues [22 ,26 ]. Contrarily, 

DM medicines may result in fluid retention, weight gain, and hy-

poglycemia. The treatment of side effects becomes much more dif-

ficult in these people since the selection and dosage adjustments 

of medications must be carefully considered to balance the advan-

tages and hazards. 

Finally, the concomitant use of anti-TB and DM drugs poses a

challenge in terms of treatment adherence. Both TB and DM ne-

cessitate protracted periods of therapy, which frequently last for 

several months or even years. Patients may become confused and 

exhibit poor compliance because of the complexity of taking many 

drugs for various diseases. In addition, the potential overlap in var-

ious drug classes’ negative effects may increase the number of pills 

needed to maintain compliance. To avoid treatment failure, the de-

velopment of medication resistance, and ensuring the overall suc-

cess of therapy, it is essential to address treatment adherence. 

Future perspective 

Meeting the unmet needs: advancing tuberculosis screening for 

diabetes mellitus 

The absence of established guidelines for TB patients being 

tested for diabetes makes it difficult to establish exact diagnostic 

criteria. Lu et al. [33 ] advised using HbA1c test rather than de-

pending on fasting/random blood glucose testing (FBG/RBG). Some 

doctors argue that 2-hr post-prandial glucose testing is the best 

method, as it is inexpensive, quick, and easy to be done compared 

to HbA1c and FBG. This disagreement makes it difficult to compare 

data across situations and hinders accurate diagnosis. 

Several studies demonstrated the benefits of implementing rou-

tine screening for DM among TB patients [6,7,23 ]. Early identifica-

tion of DM in TB patients can lead to better clinical outcomes, as 

well as prevent complications associated with this metabolic dis-

order. Current evidence suggests that the susceptibility to TB is 

higher among individuals with DM, and this increased susceptibil-

ity can make it more difficult for them to recover from the disease 

[16 ,26 ,32 ]. Diabetics may experience TB that presents differently or 

atypically and may go unnoticed or untreated [23 ,34 ]. This is due 

to a number of factors, including the fact that DM is rarely sus-

pected or recognized in TB patients due to similar clinical symp-

toms [23 ]. The symptoms of DM, such as fatigue, weight loss, and 

increased thirst, can be like those of TB [23 ], making it difficult to 

diagnose DM accurately when a patient is already diagnosed with 

TB. Both diseases involve the activation of B-cells which elicits the 

symptoms mentioned. 

TB disease typically has a slow onset and progression, owing 

to the bacilli replicating once every 18-24 hours, a much longer 

period than most pathogenic bacteria. It is well established that 

poor glycemic management helps the survival and proliferation 

of the bacteria. A recent study indicated a relational link be-

tween uncontrolled DM and increased bacterial load as well as 

a high-risk factor for cavitary lesions in TB-diabetic individuals 

[34 ]. Other investigations confirmed this finding [14 ,16 ], and it was 

commonly assumed that pulmonary TB in DM individuals had an 

unusual radiological pattern and distribution [14 ]. It is still un-

clear if DM individuals have a peculiar radiological representation 

of pulmonary TB, hence it is crucial that we prioritize the screen-

ing of TB patients for DM to provide comprehensive and efficient 

therapy. 

Multi-pronged interventions that target both TB and DM, as 

well as their underlying risk factors, are urgently needed to ad-

dress this public health challenge. 

Tuberculosis preventive therapy for diabetes cures 

The landscape for TB and DM research has progressed since 

the 2009 WHO, World Diabetes Foundation and the International 

Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung diseases expert meeting on 

TB and DM (../../TheUnion_Brief_Prevention.pdf). One of the key 

highlights of the meeting was to launch intensive research on tu-

berculosis preventive therapy for diabetic patients. Although such 

studies were not given high priority, the case for TB preven-

tive therapy is increasing recently. The WHO End TB strategy 

prioritise TB preventive therapy (TPT) for TB high risk groups 

which are mainly people living with HIV to the neglect of DM 

patients. 

The WHO advocates that all HIV-infected individuals should un-

dergo TPT irrespective of the TB diagnosis outcome since current 

diagnostic devices for TB have a lower sensitivity in people with 

advanced HIV [35 ]. A one-month regimen combination of daily ri-

fapentine and isoniazid has been reported to be effective for HIV-

infected individuals; this is one of the multiple TPT strategies avail-

able [11 ]. Similarly, isoniazid preventive treatment (IPT) or isoni-

azid prophylaxis has taken a contentious but solid stance in the 

prevention of TB in DM patients. IPT was found to lower the in-

cidence of TB in DM patients relative to placebo or no therapy in 

earlier research by Lesnichii and Karpina [36 ], albeit this finding 

was later questioned due to poor study design. There is a dearth 

of information regarding the use of IPT in diabetic individuals, but 

a current clinical trial (ClinicalTrials.govNCT04600167) is thought 

to offer the first proof supporting or disproving the use of IPT in 

TB patients with DM. 

Current guidelines, however, do not recommend IPT for DM 

patients [35 ], possibly due to the fear of developing drug resis-

tance and/or the anti-tubercular effects on metformin reported 

in studies. Evidence from an observational study postulated that 

metformin prescription might decrease the chances of diabetics 

from developing TB infection [31 ]. Two independent study pro-

posed that metformin has an encouraging anti-TB trend on var-

ious treatment outcomes, notably elevated TB treatment success, 

decreased TB mortality, increased sputum culture conversion, and 

inhibition of latent TB infection to active TB conversion [31 ,37 ]. 

Also, the standard course of TB treatment could be shortened with 

the administration of metformin [23 ,31 ]. Yu X. et al. [38 ], in a sys-

tematic analysis encompassing 12 observational studies observed 

that metformin use is related with benefits in both prevention and 

treatment outcomes of TB among people with DM. The anti-TB 

effects of metformin is known to hinder intracellular growth of 

MTB through an AMPK (adenosine monophosphate-activated pro-

tein kinase)-dependent pathway. All these anti-TB effects of met-

formin might be likely reasons why there is hesitation concerning 

TPT regimens for TB-DM prevention, like the case of TB-HIV. This 

hesitation might be compounded by the fact that metformin al-

ready confers some level of protection against TB infection [30 ]. 

Despite this, a prospective clinical study is required to stress these 

beneficial effects of metformin. 

Indeed, the TB-DM association is preventable with early screen-

ing, adherence to medication, a more robust TB vaccine [35 ], a

healthy diet, and lifestyle modification in TB endemic areas. Be-

sides, TPT for diabetes cure has the potential to improve out-

comes in individuals with DM and reduce the burden of disease 

on healthcare systems. This approach has been shown to reduce 

the risk of developing active TB, improve glycaemic control, and 

enhance overall health outcomes in individuals with DM. While

Concluding remarks 

Overall, recognizing the bidirectional relationship between TB 

and DM is crucial as it may give a clear picture of the pathophys-

iology and treatment outcome of these two diseases if acquired 

together or one preceding the other [29 ]. Strategies that leverage 

integrated management of TB and DM, such as screening and treat-

ment of both diseases, can reduce the morbidity and mortality 

rates associated with TB and DM. Similarly, identifying the specific 

mechanisms through which cortisol impairs glucose metabolism 

and immune function can guide the development of targeted in-

terventions to alleviate the burden caused by the disease conver-

gence. The global health community must work together to ad-

a b s t r a c t

The double burden of tuberculosis (TB) and diabetes mellitus (DM) represents a major public health chal-

lenge that demands urgent and integrated approaches. The interplay between these two chronic condi-

tions presents unique clinical and public health management challenges, as well as social and economic 

implications. We explored the bidirectional relationship between TB and DM, emphasizing how DM in-

creases susceptibility to TB and complicates its management, while TB may exacerbate glycemic control 

in diabetic patients. This review underscores the challenges associated with the management of both 

diseases, obstacles in screening TB patients for DM and TB preventive therapy for DM since inadequate 

glycemic control can impact treatment outcomes. Several studies have investigated the disease interplay; 

however, the results have been equivocal, and this may be exerting negative impacts on the disease pre-

vention and treatment. TB-diabetes comorbidity has been linked to poor treatment outcomes whereas TB 

prevention in people with DM at present is a dilemma. In addition to highlighting how urgent it is to 

address this comorbidity, this review offers a road map for better prevention, treatment, and control of 

several factors underlying the TB-diabetes syndemic interaction.

Introduction 

The global burden of tuberculosis (TB) and diabetes melli-

tus (DM) is substantial, and these diseases disproportionately af-

fect the most vulnerable populations, including people living in 

poverty, malnourished individuals, and the aged. TB remains a sig-

nificant global health challenge despite sustained efforts to pre-

vent, detect, and treat the disease [1]. It is the 13th cause of death 

worldwide and the deadliest infectious disease after COVID-19, and 

experts predict that if not controlled, it will become the world’s 

number one cause of death [1,2]. The TB situation varies signifi-

cantly across different geographical regions [2]. The highest bur-

den of TB is borne by low- and middle-income countries [3], with 

around 87% of all cases reported in sub-Saharan Africa, Asia, and 

South America.

Risk factors driving the persistence of the TB epidemic include 

host factors namely malnutrition, HIV infection, alcohol use disor-

ders, smoking, and finally DM [2]. In 2022, 2.2 million, 733 thou-

sand, and 705 thousand TB cases were associated with undernour-

ishment, drunkenness, and smoking, respectively. Similarly, HIV-

and diabetes-related TB cases were 894,0 0 0 and 369,0 0 0, respec-

tively [2]. 

Additionally, there are pathogen derived risk factors including, 

the emergence of drug-resistant strains such as multidrug resis-

tant TB (MDR-TB) and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB), and 

the ability of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) to transition from 

latent to active TB disease. The pathogen associated risk factors 

can be aggravated by challenges in delivering effective treatment 

to hard-to-reach communities, misuse of the available TB medi-

cations, and recently, the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. The 

COVID-19 pandemic strained TB control effort s, by causing disrup-

tions in healthcare services and weakened health systems that led 

to setbacks in TB detection and treatment. 

Diabetes mellitus, another disease of public health importance, 

has also increased rapidly worldwide (4). Unfortunately, the preva-

Even worse, prevalence has been rising more rapidly in low- and

diseases than in high-income countries. As of 2021, more than 

10.5% (536.6 million adults) were living with DM, and this number

Epidemiology: trends, and clinical presentation of TB-DM 

Mycobacterium tuberculosis is perhaps the most successful infec-

tious agent in current times. Despite its long history and numerous 

interventions put in place to address it, the incidence and preva-

lence of TB continues to increase. Each day, about 40 0 0 people lose 

their lives to TB and close to 28,0 0 0 people fall ill with this pre-

ventable and curable disease [1]. In 2022, the World Health Or-

ganization (WHO) estimated that 10.3 million people comprising 

of 8 million men, 3.5 million women and 1.3 million children fell 

ill with TB [2]. This represents a two-year reversal in the decline 

of the incidence of TB that was seen in the prior years and fur-

ther impedes the End TB goals. It is thus imperative to identify 

and study all factors that increase the risk of TB if the global goal 

of an 80% reduction in the incidence of TB and 90% reduction in 

deaths related to TB is to be achieved by 2030 [1]. 

Multiple studies have shown a strong association between DM 

and TB especially in low- and middle- income countries where TB 

is endemic, and the burden of DM is increasing [3-6 ]. About 95% 

of TB and 75% of the DM cases live in low- and middle-income 

countries [3,4,6]. In fact, of the ten countries with the highest 

number of DM patients worldwide, 6 are classified as “high bur-

den” for TB by the WHO, meaning they contribute to 80% of the 

TB cases worldwide [1]. The co-occurrence of TB-DM is not likely 

to decline anytime soon as DM weakens a person’s immune sys-

tem and increases the risk of getting active TB [5,6]. Similarly, TB 

causes “stress-induced hyperglycemia” and this can make the man-

agement of DM more difficult [3,5,6]. This is concerning as poor 

glycemic control has been linked to poor outcomes in TB treat-

ment. 

The global prevalence of TB-DM comorbidity ranges from 

13.73% [8] to 15.3% [7] varying from 0·1% in Latvia to 45 ·2% -

50.12% in Marshall Islands [7]. This wide variation in observations 

may be explained by the diverse nature of the diabetic popula-

tion [7,8]. Regionally, the prevalence of patients with DM and TB 

has been observed to be 19.32% in the Americas, 17.31% in Europe, 

14.62% in Southeast Asia, 13.59% in the western Pacific region, 

9.61% in the eastern Mediterranean region, and 9.30% in Africa [8]. 

The trend, as depicted from the studies spanning from 2014 to 

2024 (Table 1), indicates a steady increase in the disease preva-

lence among adults. The percentage of TB patients with DM var-

ied from 8.5% to 11% during 2016 to 2018 [9] and reaching as 

high as 45% [7,10 ], while patients in TB endemic countries like 

South Africa, Peru, Romania, and Indonesia was 12.5% according 

to a study that assessed DM status and clinical correlates in TB 

patients across these settings [11 ]. The prevalence of DM among 

TB patients in Sub-Saharan Africa was found to be 9.0% based 

on a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational stud-

ies [12 ]. This study included data from various countries in Sub-

Saharan Africa, with the highest prevalence reported in Nigeria at 

15%, followed by Tanzania at 11%, and Ethiopia at 10%. In Ghana, 

the prevalence was 9.4% among 2,990 TB patients enrolled in 2016 

[13 ]. The high prevalence of TB-DM comorbidity is linked to sev-

eral key factors, including urbanization, sedentary lifestyles, obe-

sity, population growth, and aging. These drivers are particularly 

significant in countries where TB is endemic. 

Longitudinal analysis of 163 studies reported increased TB inci-

dence in settings where DM prevalence increased over time [6]. A

systematic review of 13 observational cases globally revealed that 

DM was associated with a 3-fold increase in the incidence of pul-

monary TB (RR = 3.11, 95% CI 2.27-4.26) [5]. A South Asian study 

found that 11-24% of TB patients also have DM comorbidity, with 

variations across and within countries like India (14-25% preva-

lence) [10 ]. This increase in the risk of developing TB-DM is once 

again more evident in low- and middle-income countries [3,6,7]. 

However, even in countries with a low burden of TB, studies have 

shown that patients with DM have a higher risk of developing 

TB. DM is consistently linked to a higher risk of TB across various 

study designs and populations, with a relative risk of 3.11 and odds 

ratios ranging from 1.16 to 7.83, showing higher effect estimates in 

non-North American studies [5]. Noubiap et al. [7] highlighted a

notably higher prevalence of DM among TB patients in the North 

America and Caribbean, western Pacific, southeast Asia, and Mid-

dle East and North Africa regions compared to Africa, South and 

Central America, and Europe, as revealed in subgroup and meta-

regression analyses. In specific regions, the risk of TB associated 

with DM was found to be comparable to or even higher than that 

linked to HIV infection, underscoring the significant impact of DM 

on TB burden in those areas [3,9]. 

Clinically, DM, particularly poorly controlled DM, is associated 

with a more severe and contagious TB infection as compared to 

the general population. TB-DM is associated with an increased fre-

quency of pulmonary TB (in contrast to extra-pulmonary disease) 

as compared to other diseases that compromise the immune sys-

tem [14 ]. This may be due to a hyper-reactive cell-mediated im-

mune response to MTB in DM patients that may be sub-optimal for 

containing MTB growth within the lung, but effective for prevent-

ing its dissemination and reactivation elsewhere [15 ]. TB-DM is 

also associated with increased lung cavitations, positive direct spu-

tum smears at the time of diagnosis, fever, cough, hemoptysis, and 

false-negative tuberculin skin test results [14 ]. There is also some 

evidence that DM prolongs smear and culture positivity at the end 

of the intensive phase of the TB treatment [6,14 ]. DM is also asso-

ciated with an increased risk of treatment complications, relapse, 

and mortality [10 ,16 ]. Gautam, et al. [10 ] in a meta-analysis re-

ported that DM increases the risk of treatment failure (OR = 1.65;

95% CI 1.12, 2.44) and 1.74 (95% CI 1.21, 2.51) times higher odds 

of mortality compared to non-diabetic TB patients. Conversely, the 

relationship between drug or MDR-TB in DM remains unclear. A re-

cent systematic review involving 30 studies worldwide found that 

Tuberculosis-Diabetes Mellitus patients were 19% more likely to 

develop MDR-TB as compared to TB-non-DM patients (HR 0.81, 95% 

CI: 0.60-0.96, p < 0.001) [17 ]. Likewise, another analysis involving 

24 observational studies from 15 different countries revealed that 

DM has a significant positive association with MDR-TB (OR = 1.97, 

95% CI = 1.58-2.45, I2 = 38.2%, P value for heterogeneity = 0.031) ir-

respective of country income level, type of DM, how TB or DM was 

diagnosed, and design of primary studies [18 ]. However, two inde-

pendent studies by Ragouraman, et al. [9] and Gautam, et al. [10 ], 

in 2021 found no evidence for an increased risk of TB recurrence 

with drug resistant strains among people with DM. This empha-

sizes the need for more research into the TB-DM population. 

Host immune mechanism of TB-DM 

Pulmonary TB infection is mainly established through inhala-

tion of droplets of bacilli from an individual with active pulmonary 

TB through coughing, sneezing, talking, singing etc. Upon inhala-

tion, the bacilli interact with the bronchial epithelial cells which 

leads to a crosstalk between the MTB and the innate immune sys-

tem of the host [19 ]. Alveolar macrophages are likely the first types 

of antigen presenting cells that encounter the pathogen among 

others such as dendritic cells. After the encounter of MTB with the 

macrophages, phagocytosis takes place which leads to the uptake 

of the bacilli into phagosomes which fuse with lysosomes to form 

the phagolysosomes [20 ]. The phagolysosome functions to destroy 

the bacilli through the acidification of MTB in the phagolysosome 

by the actions of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species [20 ]. In-

fected myeloid dendritic cells travel to lymph nodes and with the 

help of neutrophils transform into mature dendritic cells. The ma-

ture dendritic cells activate lymphocytes through antigen presenta-

tion and induce adaptive immune responses [19 ]. The T cells travel 

to the lungs targeting MTB infected macrophages through the re-

lease of interferon gamma (IFN-γ ) and cytotoxic T cell where they 

stimulate an effective bactericidal response [15 ]. 

Additionally, some of the bacilli that escaped this process may 

be eliminated through the activation of vitamin-D receptors, which 

leads to the release of cathelicidin, anti-microbial peptides (AMP), 

and β-defensins, key in primary bacterial lysis [20 ,21 ]. Persons 

with deficit functions in these proteins may develop active TB, 

with the bacilli transported via the blood or lymphatic system. 

However, TB patients with comorbid DM, characterized by hy-

perglycemia and insulin resistance, often exhibit compromised im-

mune responses, predisposing them to primary TB infection or re-

activation of latent TB [19 ,20 ]. One significant contributing fac-

tor is the dysfunction of macrophages in DM, linked to cyto-

plasmic dsDNA/AIM2-associated pyroptosis, disrupting inflamma-

tory cytokine secretion, phagocytosis, chemotaxis, and immune 

defenses, thereby promoting bacterial growth and dissemination 

within the host [15 ,19 ,20 ,21 ]. Other factors may be responsible for 

the risk of TB disease among DM patients including: (1) the high 

blood glucose induces M2 polarization of macrophages instead of 

the classical M1 [19 ,21 ]. M2 macrophages functions in the control 

of host inflammation and generally supports MTB growth through 

the expression of high levels of anti-inflammatory cytokines such 

as IL-4 and IL-10. This also weakens the phagocytic ability of the 

macrophages leading to the evasion of the immune system. (2) 

Studies have shown that hyperglycemia increases the count of neu-

trophils however, there is also reduced migration of neutrophils to 

infected sites due to glycated collagen resulting from receptor gly-

cation end product on neutrophils [15 ,21 ]. There is also generally 

reduced chemotaxis, defective phagocytosis and reduced bacterici-

dal ability [15 ,21 ]. (3) The frequency of dendritic cells is also re-

duced significantly [21 ]. This reduces phagocytosis as well as the 

stimulation of CD4 T cells hence there is an overall decreased 

adaptive response to MTB infection in DM patients. (4) The fre-

quencies of Th1 and Th17 have been shown to decrease in DM 

patients due to increased frequency of Th2 that secretes IL4 [21 ]. 

Th2 is known to function to antagonize the frequencies of Th1 and 

Th17 [15 ,21 ]. Moreover, the ratio of Th1 and Th2 cytokines which 

control the secretions with each other, has been found to be gen-

erally lower in DM [19 ]. Hyperglycemia also leads to inhibited se-

cretion of IFN-γ and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) reducing 

the bactericidal effect on MTB [15 ]. This shows there is a drive to-

wards anti-inflammatory leading to reduced CD4 and CD8 T cells 

at sources of infection. This reduces the host immune response to 

the pathogen [20 ]. 

Bi-directional relationship between tuberculosis and diabetes 

mellitus 

TB and DM are mutually influential, with each condition poten-

tially affecting each other’s occurrence, presentation via a variety 

of mechanisms. The two have been described as "syndemic" be-

cause of their high co-occurrence rates, particularly in low- and 

middle-income countries [3]. On one hand, DM-related alterations 

in the respiratory system, such as impaired mucociliary clearance 

and pulmonary microangiopathy, facilitate the establishment and 

dissemination of TB bacteria in the lungs [22 ]. More importantly, 

DM increases the risk of TB infection, disease progression and 

death [13 ,16 ]. While on the other hand, TB can cause glucose in-

tolerance, worsen glycemic control [23 ], and exacerbates diabetes 

progression [16 ]. Individuals with comorbid TB tend to have more 

difficult forms of TB such as neuro tuberculosis and multidrug-

resistant TB [16 ,17 ,18 ]. This syndemic interaction highlight the ne-

cessity for a comprehensive approach that addresses both condi-

tions simultaneously in clinical management and public health in-

terventions. 

Impact of diabetes mellitus on tuberculosis 

Diabetes Mellitus Affects the Occurrence of Tuberculosis 

Biologically, DM fosters a more favorable environment for the 

conversion of latent TB infections (LTBI) into active TB disease 

(Figure 1) [11 ,15 ]. The generally accepted theory is that DM 

presents with a weakened immune system, facilitating the progres-

sion of LTBI to active TB [15 ], as explained below. This association 

is particularly relevant in non-pregnant populations, where DM, 

along with HIV infection, increases the likelihood of developing ac-

tive TB from LTBI [15 ]. Research has shown a moderately increased 

risk of LTBI in patients with DM from high TB incidence areas, sug-

gesting the need for combined screening for LTBI with other risk 

factors and comorbidities to identify high-risk groups effectively. 

There are substantial research and policy gaps in the prevention 

of TB disease in people with DM and the management of patients 

with TB-diabetes, highlighting the need for strategies such as tar-

geted vaccination programs, LTBI screening, and preventive therapy 

among DM patients. 

Elevated glucose levels in hyperglycemia create an environment 

conducive to MTB growth [21 ], promoting TB development in dia-

betic patients by affecting immune responses and generating Ad-

vanced Glycation End products (AGE) and chronic inflammation, 

increasing susceptibility to pathogens [21 ,23 ]. This increased TB 

burden in DM patients is attributed to the availability of sugars 

like trehalose, pyruvate, and glycerol, enabling MTB to evade host 

metabolic defenses and establish a favorable niche for growth and 

replication [21 ].

DM is associated with reduced levels of essential cytokines 

crucial for controlling MTB growth, such as IFN-γ and TNF-α

[20 ,21 ,24 ]. Macrophages from diabetic individuals exhibit dimin-

ished secretion of inflammatory cytokines like IL-1 β and TNF-

## α. The co-occurrence of DM and TB is associated with height-

ened systemic levels of proinflammatory cytokines, including IL-

1β, IL-6, and IL-18, alongside anti-inflammatory cytokines like IL-

10 [24 ]. Prolonged exposure to high glucose sensitizes macrophage 

responses to cytokine stimuli while reducing their phagocytic ac-

tivity, possibly due to metabolic pathway alterations [21 ]. Impaired 

immune response and reduced killing of intracellular bacteria in 

DM patients potentially increase bacterial load, chronic inflamma-

tion, and facilitate bacterial dissemination and severe forms of TB, 

emphasizing the importance of understanding the immunological 

and biochemical basis of TB susceptibility in DM patients for de-

veloping rational strategies to alleviate the dual burden of these 

diseases. 

Also, the microvascular complications of DM, such as impaired 

blood flow and poor tissue oxygenation in nephropathic situa-

tions, create hypoxic conditions that favor MTB survival. Lastly, the 

chronic inflammation caused by DM (redox imbalance stress) ex-

acerbates lung damage caused by TB, promoting a favorable envi-

ronment for MTB growth and exacerbating disease severity. 

There is the need for more basic immunological and clinical 

studies to the underlying mechanism of increased susceptibility to 

progression from latent mycobacterial infection to disease as well 

as negative outcomes of TB treatment. Also of equal importance 

is pharmacological studies to investigate the interaction between 

antidiabetic medication and that of TB. These studies are crucial 

as they have the potential to offer understanding and explore new 

therapeutic options for managing individuals with co-morbidity. 

Impact of diabetes mellitus on tuberculosis treatment outcome 

DM can lead to late reporting of TB. The common symptoms 

shared between DM and TB, such as weight loss and fatigue [23 ], 

can make TB undetected for longer periods, leading to delays in TB 

diagnosis and treatment initiation. 

Similarly, diabetic individuals may present with atypical radio-

logical findings as compared with TB patients without DM [14 ,23 ]. 

Diabetics typically experience abnormal radiographic patterns like 

miliary TB, lower lobe infiltrates, cavitation in the middle and up-

per lung zones, pleural effusion, and pulmonary nodules with cen-

tral low attenuation. When managing diabetics who are also TB 

coinfected, it is essential to recognize these unusual radiological 

abnormalities to make an accurate diagnosis and arrange an effi-

cient course of therapy. 

The coexistence of DM and TB can lead to decreased drug ab-

sorption (pined to altered gut motility, and impaired intestinal per-

meability), altered metabolism of anti-TB drugs, and reduced host 

response to treatment. Diabetes-related neuropathy often affects 

the enteric nervous system, leading to compromised gut motility 

and subsequent delayed drug absorption. Moreover, hyperglycemia 

in DM can alter gut permeability through the disruption of tight 

junction proteins [22 ]. This disrupted integrity allows for increased 

penetration of the MTB pathogens and hinders adequate absorp-

tion of the TB medications. 

Thus, individuals with DM have been reported to be more 

prone to treatment failure, relapse, and drug resistance [13 ,16 ,

17 ,18 ]. 

Compromised liver function resulting from both DM and TB fur-

ther exacerbates drug metabolism issues. Rifampin, a key anti-TB 

drug, can induce liver enzyme-cytochrome P450 and transporters-

P glycoproteins that metabolize oral anti-diabetic agents [25 ], and 

subsequently reduce the therapeutic concentrations and efficacies. 

This further leads to hyperglycemia which further worsens TB thus 

creating a vicious cycle. As a result, individuals with DM may have 

a slower response to anti-TB drugs and a higher risk of treatment 

failure or relapse. One study suggested that individuals with DM 

may require a longer duration of TB treatment to achieve success-

ful outcomes [9], contributing to increased healthcare costs and 

patient burden. 

Individuals with DM may be susceptible to hepatotoxicity, a

potential side effect of isoniazid and rifampin [26 ]. Diabetics are 

more prone to this because of the pre-existing liver involvement 

or compromised metabolic pathways with the use of both medica-

tions [26 ]. Lastly, the comorbidity of DM and TB can lead to higher 

mortality rates compared to either disease alone. This is attributed 

to the synergistic impact of impaired immune response, delayed 

diagnosis, increased treatment complications, and overall compro-

mised health. 

Effects of tuberculosis on diabetes mellitus 

The link between TB and DM was demonstrated in research 

where about 42.6% of active TB patients were reported to have im-

paired glucose tolerance that resolved following TB therapy [27 ]. 

Even though this hyperglycemia is transient, it can complicate the 

diagnosis of DM in TB patients. Patients may either be misdi-

agnosed with DM and thus may be exposed to the side effects 

of anti glycemic agents. In addition, failure to perform follow-up 

DM testing may miss individuals whose insulin resistance may 

worsen following TB treatment. TB can also lead to the develop-

ment of diabetes in several ways. First, hematological spread of 

bacilli from the primary pulmonary TB site can cause direct inva-

sion to other organs, for example, pancreas. The inflammatory re-

sponse mounted against TB can damage pancreatic beta cells, fur-

ther hampering insulin secretion and aggravating glucose home-

ostasis [28 ]. The radiological features resemble pancreatic malig-

nancy or pancreatitis [28 ], which in each case impair the correct 

function of the pancreas, that is, the production of insulin for the 

regulation of excess blood sugar. In all circumstances, the pancreas 

fails to release enough insulin, which causes blood sugar to build 

up and ultimately induce DM. 

Also, long standing TB infections often lead to chronic inflam-

mation, which can induce metabolic stress that may lead to the 

release of cortisol [29 ,30 ], a stress hormone produced in response 

to infection and chronic diseases. Cortisol suppresses the activity 

of T-cells, which are vital in controlling infections. Both TB and 

DM activate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, which 

may lead to increased cortisol production [30 ]. Chronically elevated 

cortisol levels exacerbate insulin resistance and impair glucose 

metabolism in individuals with DM [29 ,30 ], worsening glycemic 

control. This prolonged exposure to high cortisol levels weakens 

the immune system’s ability to fight infections, making individ-

uals more susceptible to TB infection and impairing their abil-

ity to clear the TB bacilli. This metabolic stress induced by cor-

tisol contributes to the reactivation of latent TB, further compro-

mising the health outcomes of affected individuals. Further de-

velopment of DM leads to compromises in the immune system 

stability and the cycle continues over and over as modeled in 

experiment. 

Challenges associated with the management of TB-DM Comorbid 

Individuals 

TB and DM can be treated simultaneously. Treating both condi-

tions concurrently is vital to ensure optimal outcomes for these pa-

tients, as untreated diabetes can compromise the immune system 

and effectiveness of TB treatment. Controlling blood glucose levels 

in patients with DM is essential to enhance optimal TB treatment 

[16 ,21 ,23 ]. In addition to lifestyle modifications, DM is managed by 

hypoglycemic agents such as metformin, sulfonylureas, DPP-4 in-

hibitors insulin therapy. Treating TB promptly with appropriate an-

tibiotics is crucial in preventing the worsening of diabetes control. 

However, treating patients with both TB and DM can prove to be 

complex and challenging due to the intricate relationship between 

these two diseases and some of the medications involved. The con-

ventional treatment regimen for drug susceptible new TB cases is 

isoniazid (H), rifampin (R), pyrazinamide (Z), and ethambutol (E) 

taken over a period of 6 months, taken under supervision. This ap-

proach, known as directly observed therapy short-course (DOTS), 

has proven to be effective in curing the disease. 

The possibility of drug-drug interactions between these two 

medications is one of the main difficulties. Most of the interactions 

are related to induction of cytochrome enzymes, which may lead 

to reduction in either the anti-diabetic agents or the anti-TB drugs, 

compromising their effectiveness and worsening the treatment 

outcomes in such individuals. Anti-TB medications like rifampin 

have the potential to induce liver enzymes [14 ], which could speed 

up the metabolism of diabetic medications and diminish their 

effectiveness [25 ]. Rifam picin through enzyme induction acceler-

ates the metabolism of sulfonylurea and biguanides reducing their 

plasma levels and thus leading to poor glucose control. Isoniazid 

may also antagonize the effect of sulfonylureas, also worsening 

glucose control. These drugs however do have an effect on the 

metabolism of insulin and as such the patients with active TB in-

fection may be forced to switch to using insulin despite its higher 

cost. Moreover, isoniazid and rifampin, the 2 key medications for 

sterilization against the MTB are known to be potent inducers 

and transporters of several anti-diabetic agents [25 ,26 ]. Rifampin 

is known to induce uridinediphosphate-glucuronosyl-transferases 

as well as influx and efflux important transporters including P-

glycoprotein in the liver, kidney, and erythrocytic cells that can af-

fect the metabolism of many medications including sulfonylureas, 

HIV protease inhibitors, and HIV nonnucleoside reverse transcrip-

tase inhibitors [25 ,26 ]. 

Anti-DM medications can also influence availability of anti-TB 

medications. The sulfonylureas and isoniazid are both metabolized 

in the liver by CYP2C9, so co-administration could increase isoni-

azid concentration levels in blood circulation. Due to this, sulfony-

lureas are discouraged in patients receiving anti-TB therapy [26 ]. 

Interestingly, metformin bypasses hepatic metabolism. Instead, it is 

absorbed by members of the solute carrier family via the organic 

cation transporter subtype 1 (OCT1) and eliminated unchanged by 

OCT2 in the kidneys. This unique pathway leads to minimal inter-

actions with anti-TB medications [31 ]. 

Metformin has a lesser effect on cytochrome P450 enzyme-

induced metabolism. In addition, it has been demonstrated to 

shorten the duration of TB treatment [23 ,31 ]. Metformin-exposed 

macrophages exhibited higher bactericidal activity because of in-

creased production of reactive oxidative species (ROS) required to 

eliminate bacteria in the mitochondria [31 ]. 

Only limited studies have been conducted to explore the cure 

rates of patients with both TB and DM, leaving the issue largely 

unexplored. Several studies that investigated the cure rates of TB 

patients with DM reveal a wide range of outcomes [16 ,17 ,32 ]. One 

research indicates that these patients have relatively lower cure 

rates compared to individuals without DM [32 ]. Factors contribut-

ing to this disparity include altered immune responses, altered gut 

motility and drug metabolism due to diabetes complications, and 

increased severity of TB symptoms, due to suboptimal glucose con-

trol.

A significant additional challenge is the increased likelihood of 

adverse effects and treatment challenges brought on by the con-

comitant use of both medications. When administered together, 

the side effects of TB and DM medications frequently overlap. Pa-

tients taking anti-TB drugs run the risk of developing drug-induced 

neuropathies, hepatotoxicity, or digestive issues [22 ,26 ]. Contrarily, 

DM medicines may result in fluid retention, weight gain, and hy-

poglycemia. The treatment of side effects becomes much more dif-

ficult in these people since the selection and dosage adjustments 

of medications must be carefully considered to balance the advan-

tages and hazards. 

Finally, the concomitant use of anti-TB and DM drugs poses a

challenge in terms of treatment adherence. Both TB and DM ne-

cessitate protracted periods of therapy, which frequently last for 

several months or even years. Patients may become confused and 

exhibit poor compliance because of the complexity of taking many 

drugs for various diseases. In addition, the potential overlap in var-

ious drug classes’ negative effects may increase the number of pills 

needed to maintain compliance. To avoid treatment failure, the de-

velopment of medication resistance, and ensuring the overall suc-

cess of therapy, it is essential to address treatment adherence. 

Future perspective 

Meeting the unmet needs: advancing tuberculosis screening for 

diabetes mellitus 

The absence of established guidelines for TB patients being 

tested for diabetes makes it difficult to establish exact diagnostic 

criteria. Lu et al. [33 ] advised using HbA1c test rather than de-

pending on fasting/random blood glucose testing (FBG/RBG). Some 

doctors argue that 2-hr post-prandial glucose testing is the best 

method, as it is inexpensive, quick, and easy to be done compared 

to HbA1c and FBG. This disagreement makes it difficult to compare 

data across situations and hinders accurate diagnosis. 

Several studies demonstrated the benefits of implementing rou-

tine screening for DM among TB patients [6,7,23 ]. Early identifica-

tion of DM in TB patients can lead to better clinical outcomes, as 

well as prevent complications associated with this metabolic dis-

order. Current evidence suggests that the susceptibility to TB is 

higher among individuals with DM, and this increased susceptibil-

ity can make it more difficult for them to recover from the disease 

[16 ,26 ,32 ]. Diabetics may experience TB that presents differently or 

atypically and may go unnoticed or untreated [23 ,34 ]. This is due 

to a number of factors, including the fact that DM is rarely sus-

pected or recognized in TB patients due to similar clinical symp-

toms [23 ]. The symptoms of DM, such as fatigue, weight loss, and 

increased thirst, can be like those of TB [23 ], making it difficult to 

diagnose DM accurately when a patient is already diagnosed with 

TB. Both diseases involve the activation of B-cells which elicits the 

symptoms mentioned. 

TB disease typically has a slow onset and progression, owing 

to the bacilli replicating once every 18-24 hours, a much longer 

period than most pathogenic bacteria. It is well established that 

poor glycemic management helps the survival and proliferation 

of the bacteria. A recent study indicated a relational link be-

tween uncontrolled DM and increased bacterial load as well as 

a high-risk factor for cavitary lesions in TB-diabetic individuals 

[34 ]. Other investigations confirmed this finding [14 ,16 ], and it was 

commonly assumed that pulmonary TB in DM individuals had an 

unusual radiological pattern and distribution [14 ]. It is still un-

clear if DM individuals have a peculiar radiological representation 

of pulmonary TB, hence it is crucial that we prioritize the screen-

ing of TB patients for DM to provide comprehensive and efficient 

therapy. 

Multi-pronged interventions that target both TB and DM, as 

well as their underlying risk factors, are urgently needed to ad-

dress this public health challenge. 

Tuberculosis preventive therapy for diabetes cures 

The landscape for TB and DM research has progressed since 

the 2009 WHO, World Diabetes Foundation and the International 

Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung diseases expert meeting on 

TB and DM (../../TheUnion_Brief_Prevention.pdf). One of the key 

highlights of the meeting was to launch intensive research on tu-

berculosis preventive therapy for diabetic patients. Although such 

studies were not given high priority, the case for TB preven-

tive therapy is increasing recently. The WHO End TB strategy 

prioritise TB preventive therapy (TPT) for TB high risk groups 

which are mainly people living with HIV to the neglect of DM 

patients. 

The WHO advocates that all HIV-infected individuals should un-

dergo TPT irrespective of the TB diagnosis outcome since current 

diagnostic devices for TB have a lower sensitivity in people with 

advanced HIV [35 ]. A one-month regimen combination of daily ri-

fapentine and isoniazid has been reported to be effective for HIV-

infected individuals; this is one of the multiple TPT strategies avail-

able [11 ]. Similarly, isoniazid preventive treatment (IPT) or isoni-

azid prophylaxis has taken a contentious but solid stance in the 

prevention of TB in DM patients. IPT was found to lower the in-

cidence of TB in DM patients relative to placebo or no therapy in 

earlier research by Lesnichii and Karpina [36 ], albeit this finding 

was later questioned due to poor study design. There is a dearth 

of information regarding the use of IPT in diabetic individuals, but 

a current clinical trial (ClinicalTrials.govNCT04600167) is thought 

to offer the first proof supporting or disproving the use of IPT in 

TB patients with DM. 

Current guidelines, however, do not recommend IPT for DM 

patients [35 ], possibly due to the fear of developing drug resis-

tance and/or the anti-tubercular effects on metformin reported 

in studies. Evidence from an observational study postulated that 

metformin prescription might decrease the chances of diabetics 

from developing TB infection [31 ]. Two independent study pro-

posed that metformin has an encouraging anti-TB trend on var-

ious treatment outcomes, notably elevated TB treatment success, 

decreased TB mortality, increased sputum culture conversion, and 

inhibition of latent TB infection to active TB conversion [31 ,37 ]. 

Also, the standard course of TB treatment could be shortened with 

the administration of metformin [23 ,31 ]. Yu X. et al. [38 ], in a sys-

tematic analysis encompassing 12 observational studies observed 

that metformin use is related with benefits in both prevention and 

treatment outcomes of TB among people with DM. The anti-TB 

effects of metformin is known to hinder intracellular growth of 

MTB through an AMPK (adenosine monophosphate-activated pro-

tein kinase)-dependent pathway. All these anti-TB effects of met-

formin might be likely reasons why there is hesitation concerning 

TPT regimens for TB-DM prevention, like the case of TB-HIV. This 

hesitation might be compounded by the fact that metformin al-

ready confers some level of protection against TB infection [30 ]. 

Despite this, a prospective clinical study is required to stress these 

beneficial effects of metformin. 

Indeed, the TB-DM association is preventable with early screen-

ing, adherence to medication, a more robust TB vaccine [35 ], a

healthy diet, and lifestyle modification in TB endemic areas. Be-

sides, TPT for diabetes cure has the potential to improve out-

comes in individuals with DM and reduce the burden of disease 

on healthcare systems. This approach has been shown to reduce 

the risk of developing active TB, improve glycaemic control, and 

enhance overall health outcomes in individuals with DM. While

Concluding remarks 

Overall, recognizing the bidirectional relationship between TB 

and DM is crucial as it may give a clear picture of the pathophys-

iology and treatment outcome of these two diseases if acquired 

together or one preceding the other [29 ]. Strategies that leverage 

integrated management of TB and DM, such as screening and treat-

ment of both diseases, can reduce the morbidity and mortality 

rates associated with TB and DM. Similarly, identifying the specific 

mechanisms through which cortisol impairs glucose metabolism 

and immune function can guide the development of targeted in-

terventions to alleviate the burden caused by the disease conver-

gence. The global health community must work together to ad-

dress this critical public health issue and improve health outcomes 

for those affected by TB and DM.

# Antibiotic Awareness: Ensuring Pharmaceutical Care in Ghana

11 November 2019

![Image 1: Image](https://www.globalhealthpartnerships.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/DSC03199.jpg)

## During a recent visit to Ghana we met Israel, a specialist pharmacist at Keta Municipal Hospital who is involved in the CwPAMS project, in partnership with Healthcare Improvement Scotland, to strengthen the capacity of the health workforce to tackle the growing challenge of Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR).

My name is Israel Sefah and I am a specialist pharmacist at the Keta Municipal Hospital. My work involves ensuring pharmaceutical care in the hospital. I have worked here for nine years. I wanted to study medicine when I finished my secondary education and my father advised me that it was good to study pharmacy, and now here I am!

Mine is the only available hospital in this catchment area, so we are very busy. On our busiest days we can see between 400-600 patients and on less busy days, between 200-300. Certain days are busier, for instance on a Wednesday, we have a diabetic clinic where we see around 100 patients. We also have an eye clinic, a mental health clinic, and an antenatal clinic that can see around 100 patients in a day. Then there’s the general OPD, where up to 300 patients a day are treated for different conditions.

The biggest barriers patients face are financial ones. National health insurance does not cover everything so patients might have to pay extra for a lab test, or for medicine. It is not very expensive but for a poor person, even 1 cedi is expensive. Transportation is another barrier; getting to hospital is difficult for patients who live far away. Cultural barriers also play a part – there is a lot of herbal medicine here and people’s faith and beliefs hinder them from coming to hospital for treatment. Some arrive in a very bad state, having tried other things first such going to a prayer camp. At the pharmacy, we try to educate people on the importance of coming to the hospital, but this largely happens on a one to one basis, so the message doesn’t reach everyone. We have a very strong public health unit made up of nurses who visit homes, markets, schools and other public places to educate people. Despite the barriers, there have been gains throughout the years. In the past, babies were delivered at home by traditional birth attendants and there was a belief that a caesarean section made you a bad woman, but now most mothers choose to give birth in hospital where there are qualified midwives and doctors.

The pharmacy is made up of around fourteen people, but it’s a big hospital and I’m the only one overseeing pharmacy activity across seven different clinics (including the diabetic, mental health, tuberculosis, and HIV clinics). The hospital does not have a pharmacy technician, so ensuring prudent use of medicine, one of the main roles of pharmacists, is challenging. If I attend a meeting, it means I’m not at the pharmacy. Those assisting are not technically trained, and therefore can’t judge whether a prescription is appropriate. It’s a worrying situation.

One of the problems in Ghana is that the development of healthcare isn’t even – we have a lot of nurses and doctors, but fewer pharmacists or biomedical engineers, so doctors and nurses are missing good pharmacists who can contribute to drug management and quality pharmaceutical care.

In general, we have most of the basic equipment and facilities for our level of primary care delivery, but in some wards, like the maternity ward or the obstetrics and gynaecology ward, there are not enough beds and sometimes women have to sleep on the floor. When equipment breaks down, the rate of replacement is slow, and we are sometimes without it for long periods of time, meaning that basic lab tests are not carried out. As everything is provided by central government and the hospital lacks sufficient funds to buy some of the very expensive equipment, the rate of replacement is a problem and I worry about how to ensure quality care management.

We have seen a couple of cases where patients are becoming resistant to antibiotics and we are getting to a point where most of our antibiotics won’t work. I am hoping that the rate of resistance will be reduced through the antimicrobial stewardship project. A dedicated team will collect data which we will use both to increase our awareness of antimicrobial usage and to inform decision making regarding the appropriate use of antibiotics across the hospital.

It is difficult to effect change when it is championed by just one person and in the past some staff have been resistant to change. However, as this is a team project comprising colleagues from different departments – the lab, the pharmacy, a doctor, a nurse – it should be easier to communicate with other colleagues and to generate consensus so that change is accepted by the whole team.

I find it fulfilling to contribute to quality of care and management and enjoy overcoming challenges, formulating solutions and seeing an improvement in patient outcomes. My hope for the future is that every hospital will have all of these teams working together to deliver quality care, not just on the pharmacy side, but across the hospital, to every patient.

We have seen a couple of cases where patients are becoming resistant to antibiotics and we are getting to a point where most of our antibiotics won’t work.

**Israel Sefah** - Specialist Pharmacist, Keta Municipal Hospital

# Antibiotic Awareness: Ensuring Pharmaceutical Care in Ghana

11 November 2019

![Image 1: Image](https://www.globalhealthpartnerships.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/DSC03199.jpg)

## During a recent visit to Ghana we met Israel, a specialist pharmacist at Keta Municipal Hospital who is involved in the CwPAMS project, in partnership with Healthcare Improvement Scotland, to strengthen the capacity of the health workforce to tackle the growing challenge of Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR).

My name is Israel Sefah and I am a specialist pharmacist at the Keta Municipal Hospital. My work involves ensuring pharmaceutical care in the hospital. I have worked here for nine years. I wanted to study medicine when I finished my secondary education and my father advised me that it was good to study pharmacy, and now here I am!

Mine is the only available hospital in this catchment area, so we are very busy. On our busiest days we can see between 400-600 patients and on less busy days, between 200-300. Certain days are busier, for instance on a Wednesday, we have a diabetic clinic where we see around 100 patients. We also have an eye clinic, a mental health clinic, and an antenatal clinic that can see around 100 patients in a day. Then there’s the general OPD, where up to 300 patients a day are treated for different conditions.

The biggest barriers patients face are financial ones. National health insurance does not cover everything so patients might have to pay extra for a lab test, or for medicine. It is not very expensive but for a poor person, even 1 cedi is expensive. Transportation is another barrier; getting to hospital is difficult for patients who live far away. Cultural barriers also play a part – there is a lot of herbal medicine here and people’s faith and beliefs hinder them from coming to hospital for treatment. Some arrive in a very bad state, having tried other things first such going to a prayer camp. At the pharmacy, we try to educate people on the importance of coming to the hospital, but this largely happens on a one to one basis, so the message doesn’t reach everyone. We have a very strong public health unit made up of nurses who visit homes, markets, schools and other public places to educate people. Despite the barriers, there have been gains throughout the years. In the past, babies were delivered at home by traditional birth attendants and there was a belief that a caesarean section made you a bad woman, but now most mothers choose to give birth in hospital where there are qualified midwives and doctors.

The pharmacy is made up of around fourteen people, but it’s a big hospital and I’m the only one overseeing pharmacy activity across seven different clinics (including the diabetic, mental health, tuberculosis, and HIV clinics). The hospital does not have a pharmacy technician, so ensuring prudent use of medicine, one of the main roles of pharmacists, is challenging. If I attend a meeting, it means I’m not at the pharmacy. Those assisting are not technically trained, and therefore can’t judge whether a prescription is appropriate. It’s a worrying situation.

One of the problems in Ghana is that the development of healthcare isn’t even – we have a lot of nurses and doctors, but fewer pharmacists or biomedical engineers, so doctors and nurses are missing good pharmacists who can contribute to drug management and quality pharmaceutical care.

In general, we have most of the basic equipment and facilities for our level of primary care delivery, but in some wards, like the maternity ward or the obstetrics and gynaecology ward, there are not enough beds and sometimes women have to sleep on the floor. When equipment breaks down, the rate of replacement is slow, and we are sometimes without it for long periods of time, meaning that basic lab tests are not carried out. As everything is provided by central government and the hospital lacks sufficient funds to buy some of the very expensive equipment, the rate of replacement is a problem and I worry about how to ensure quality care management.

We have seen a couple of cases where patients are becoming resistant to antibiotics and we are getting to a point where most of our antibiotics won’t work. I am hoping that the rate of resistance will be reduced through the antimicrobial stewardship project. A dedicated team will collect data which we will use both to increase our awareness of antimicrobial usage and to inform decision making regarding the appropriate use of antibiotics across the hospital.

It is difficult to effect change when it is championed by just one person and in the past some staff have been resistant to change. However, as this is a team project comprising colleagues from different departments – the lab, the pharmacy, a doctor, a nurse – it should be easier to communicate with other colleagues and to generate consensus so that change is accepted by the whole team.

I find it fulfilling to contribute to quality of care and management and enjoy overcoming challenges, formulating solutions and seeing an improvement in patient outcomes. My hope for the future is that every hospital will have all of these teams working together to deliver quality care, not just on the pharmacy side, but across the hospital, to every patient.

We have seen a couple of cases where patients are becoming resistant to antibiotics and we are getting to a point where most of our antibiotics won’t work.

**Israel Sefah** - Specialist Pharmacist, Keta Municipal Hospital
