### Implications of knowledge deficiency on glucose monitoring

The study revealed that prior to and upon diagnosis, participants lacked knowledge about their condition, mostly about its management, which includes glucose monitoring. This was revealed based on their action and inaction as described during the interview. These actions and inactions, which include non-disclosure of information on their condition and errors committed, point clearly to either a lack of knowledge, wrong information, or perception. This lack of knowledge may probably be attributed to inadequate education on clinic days. It was observed that the facility lacked infrastructure, and as a result, individuals with diabetes were in queues with different groups of clients to seek care during clinic days, creating long queues at the facility. Due to this, the health education normally given to these clients appears to be inadequate and general in nature to cater for all clients. The only time they had the opportunity to get educated specifically on their condition, which is diabetes is at the consulting room, and due to time factor, the engagement is usually limited. Lastly, it was also observed that two or more Doctors were in one consulting room, attending to different clients at the same time. The sub-themes under this theme include: nondisclosure of information on their condition and Committed errors that could have been avoided in glucose monitoring.

### Non-disclosure of information on condition

The most of the participants indicated that they did not disclose or discuss their newly diagnosed condition and its management, which includes glucose monitoring, to anybody. However, some indicated that they only disclosed it to their close relatives, whom they think could be of help to them.

A 64-year-old woman did not mince words in her failure to disclose her condition to other people except her very close relatives.

> _“No_,_I didn’t tell anybody about it!! Why should I? I only told my son because I don’t think my other family members can be of help to me in any way_,_they will only gossip about you_,_even my brother is not aware.… “(C2)_.

Another 48-year-old man added that:

> _“Laughter!! Tell who? I live alone in my house_,_my wife and kids are down south_,_and I don’t think I should worry them about this. They only know I was not well and I went to the hospital for treatment…….” (C12)_.

### Committed errors that could have been avoided in glucose monitoring

Interactions with participants also revealed that most of them made errors in one way or the other in their glucose monitoring process and its complications all because they were new to the phenomenon. What was clear was that most of these errors committed by the participants were because they did not have much knowledge of the condition and therefore had no idea they were committing an error.

A 52-year-old man indicated that:

> _“Hmmm… it was serious and funny; I was discharged two weeks ago. I didn’t understand the nurse well. Initially_,_I thought that after one month_,_if my sugar level was down_,_there was no need to come back. I was happy and started eating my normal food until I started feeling unwell again and was rushed here_,_only to be informed that my sugar level had risen again. What kind of sickness is this?“(C6)_.

Some even observed others and ended up committing errors, for instance, a 68-year-old male pensioner said;

> _“I thought the review was only necessary when my sugar level is high_,_because I saw some people here last three months ago_,_but the following month_,_I didn’t see them again_,_so I thought if I felt better_,_I could stay away from the review. That is why I didn’t come for review last month_,_I even argued with my daughter over it” (C10)_.

Several of them confessed that they were not able to identify the symptoms of impending hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia at home. At the time of interacting with them, most of them were now able to tell when they were running into either hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia. All the participants admitted that they initially did not know about it.

According to a 67-year-old woman, there were a couple of times she mistook hypoglycemia for hyperglycemia and took her medication earlier than the stipulated time, and even nearly increased her dose of medication that day, all because she did not know and was not monitoring her glucose level regularly.

> _“That day I woke up early in the morning feeling dizzy_,_and my heart was beating fast with some tremors in my lower limbs_,_I was even scared to get up and walk. I thought my sugar level was high_,_so I took my drug earlier than the usual time. I even wanted to increase the number of tablets.” After taking the medicine_,_it was becoming worse. I had to go to the nearby clinic where I was told that my sugar level was rather low……” (C11)_.

Over time, most of the participants began to learn the signs of hyper- and hypoglycemia.

> _“I used not to know and always thought it was the side effects of the medication_,_which made me even stop taking it some time ago_,_I think for one week_,_that was last two months or so_,_but now I know that when I have blur vision or thirst_,_it means my sugar level is rising and when I have dizziness and sweating it also means my sugar level is going low….”(C 14)_.

Most of the participants who committed errors in their management process, including monitoring of their sugar level, attribute it to a lack of understanding on their part, associated with a lack of attention and education to them as new clients

> _“My appointment is supposed to be next two weeks_,_I am back because my sugar level is still high. I was eating every type of food except sugar_,_I didn’t understand. I didn’t also want to ask because I was with other people_,_I wish I had the opportunity to ask her that day_,_like by now I wouldn’t be back here today“(C5)_.

### Social and environmental determinants of glucose monitoring

One of the most difficult aspects of glucose monitoring as a lifestyle modification management is the numerous social and environmental factors associated with it. This appeared not to be different from individuals newly diagnosed with diabetes. All participants in this study had one challenge or another in relation to their glucose monitoring practices. It was found that most of the participants do not own glucometers. These participants without glucometers had to face the inconvenience of visiting the facility regularly for monitoring or alternatively pay more at private facilities to have their glucose level checked. Even the few with glucometers were also faced with the cost of purchasing glucometer strips, which still hindered their regular monitoring. The sub-themes under this theme include: Barriers to regular blood glucose monitoring, and Resource support from families and spiritual leaders.

### Barriers to regular blood glucose monitoring

When it comes to glucose monitoring, the challenges or barriers were found to include the following: the fear of needle prick, cost of monitoring, distance to health centers and pharmacists where they can have access to glucose monitoring, feeling reluctant after sugar level is normalized and lack of trust for some results outside the facility.

> _“I was having the machine but it was giving me high_,_high figures I didn’t trust the results that is why I always come here (the hospital) and here (the hospital) too because of the distance_,_I am unable to monitor it daily.” (C1)_.
> 
> 
> _“I always prefer doing it here because the results I get by doing it myself_,_I don’t trust it_,_my figures are always high.” (C8)_.

A few of the participants have glucometers but the cost of buying strips also served as an obstacle to regular monitoring.

> _“My son bought it for me but I don’t have money to buy the strips in bulk_,_anytime I am able to buy them_,_I always do the monitoring myself at home.” (C13)_.

Some participants were also confronted with peculiar challenges such as fear of needle pricks and access to glucose monitoring services.

> _“I have fear for the needle so it’s always not easy for me_,_I do check but not as frequently as am supposed to.” (C9)_.
> 
> 
> _“It’s only when I come here (the hospital) that I check_,_my place is far from town so it’s not easy getting a pharmacy to do it.” (C13)_.

#### Resource support from families and spiritual leaders

Almost all participants indicated that they do not get any form of physical or material support elsewhere apart from their immediate family. Some indicated that the only financial support they sometimes get outside the family is from their spiritual leaders. They were all of the view that they would need support, especially with the cost involved and access to glucose monitoring. Most of them indicated that they do not get any direct support from anywhere, including the government, except from their close relations, such as children and spouses.

> _“No!! I don’t get any support from anywhere except my son_,_or is there any support somewhere that I don’t know?” (C1)_.
> 
> 
> _“It’s my son who bears all the cost and sometimes when my brother comes around_,_then he gives me something. Nobody else supports me” (C7)_.
> 
> 
> _Sometimes my pastor buys some of the drugs for me. He is the one who even bought my glucometer strips for me last week when it got finished. God will bless him for me” (C2)_.

The most of the participants prefer that any form of support be channeled towards the cost of their medication, the cost of glucometer strips, or the cost of blood glucose monitoring.

> _“My main problem is buying the medicine and paying for them to check my sugar level_,_if the government can help us there_,_we will be ok“(C5)_.

### Incentives and motivational drivers shaping glucose monitoring behaviors

The study again revealed some drivers that kept individuals newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes going despite all the challenges they encountered preceding their diagnosis. The sub-themes under this include: the need to stay alive for the shake of their dependents, the hope to one day do without some lifestyle modification, benefits gained from adherence to regular glucose monitoring and motivation from family members spiritual leaders and care providers.

#### The need to stay alive for the sake of dependents

It was observed that most participants draw their motivation from the fact that they have dependents who look up to them.

> _“Pricking myself all the time and not being able to eat certain kinds of foods is not easy_,_but once you have to do that to stay healthy_,_I have to do it because my children are still young and I need to stay alive to raise them.“(C15)_.

From a similar angle, a 43-year-old woman also added that:

> _“As I said earlier_,_this is the condition that killed my mother_,_so I want to make sure I stay alive to cater for my children.“(C13)_.
> 
> 
> _“They say life begins at 40_,_so I have just begun life_,_why will I want to die…laughter….”(C4)_.

#### The hope to one day do without some lifestyle modification

Some of the participants were hoping that one day, their glucose level would be normalized so that they would be free from having to check or take medication every day.

> _“I am doing my best to follow what the doctor said_,_I am hoping that one day_,_he (Doctor) will ask me to stop the medication because my sugar level is normal.”(C14)_.

Some participants, though hoped to get better someday; their hope was with a divine intervention:

> _“I am following the treatment_,_and I pray that one day_,_my God will perform a miracle”(C8)_.
> 
> 
> _“I know I will be fine one day_,_but there is a saying that God helps those who help themselves; that is why I want to follow everything [exactly as directed] to see if God will help me one day”(C2)_.

#### Benefits gained from adherence to regular glucose monitoring

Most participants get results from adhering to the lifestyle modifications, including glucose monitoring, which serves as a motivation for them to continue. Feeling better and seeing improvement in the results when monitoring their glucose level motivates them to continue to do more. Most participants who adhered to regular glucose monitoring attributed it to their improved results. Ironically, it was also found that, improved glucose reading led a few participants to become complacent resulting in relaxed attitude and discontinuation of regular monitoring.

> _“After adhering to the instructions from the doctor for a few days_,_I can feel it myself inside that I feel fine_,_so it’s helping me.“(C4)_.
> 
> 
> _" I was still taking small_,_small…. laughter….it’s not easy to just stop at once like that_,_but ever since I stopped drinking completely_,_I felt so well and normal_,_so never will I go back to drinking again.“(C7)_.
> 
> 
> _“Whenever I check my sugar level and realize it’s stable and am getting better_,_I feel happy and want to do more to keep it.”(C9)_.

#### Motivation from family, spiritual leaders and care providers

Several of the participants also attribute their source of motivation to their formal caregivers as well as their immediate family members.

A 67-year-old woman showered all the praises on her son as her only source of motivation:

> _“Is my son who is doing everything for me_,_he encourages me and he buys all my medication for me_,_for my son!!! [especially] I will say he is my only source or motivation.”(C11)_.

Similarly, a 68-year-old male cited his daughter as his source of motivation and encouragement.

> _“Is my daughter who motivates me otherwise I would have stopped this up and down_,_at this my age why will I fear death again_,_she has been bringing me and encouraging me to take my medication.”(C10)_.

Some participants also get encouragement and motivation from healthcare providers

> _“There was one fair doctor here_,_I have forgotten his name today I didn’t see him_,_he was the one I was free with and always express myself well. Oh!! He was doing well; he was always encouraging me to follow the treatment” (C1)_.
> 
> 
> _“The doctor who I have been seeing is always not happy when I come and my sugar level is not stable_,_because of that I always want to make sure it’s better on my next visit.”(C9)_.

Several of them also indicated that they sometimes get prayers and encouragement outside the family from their spiritual leaders

> _“my pastor also doesn’t forget me in prayers_,_he prays for me every day and I think that is helping me a lot” (C2)_.
> 
> 
> _“In fact I was sad but my pastor encouraged to be faithful and trust in God_,_I giving evry thing to God and I know I will fine”(C8)_.

## Discussion

### Implication of knowledge deficiency on glucose monitoring

The findings of this study revealed that most of the participants lacked knowledge about glucose monitoring practices, revealing a critical failure in patient education at the point of diagnosis. This affected their glucose monitoring behaviours and practices. These findings are comparable to the findings of Nguyen and colleagues (2020), which say that the knowledge and attitude of individuals with diabetes were just a little above average when it comes to knowing about the condition [10]. The methodology employed for both studies, however, is not the same, making it difficult for the results of this study to be quantified as done in the previous study, since this was a qualitative study. This study, however, revealed in-depth information that found education on conditions in the setting to be inadequate, as care providers on clinic days were consistently overwhelmed by the number of clients they had to attend to. These numbers were always high because care providers also used those days to attend to other groups of clients besides individuals with diabetes, leading to long queues. Additionally, due to the mixture of individuals with various conditions, the health education typically provided is more general and not disease-specific. Improving human resources, expanding infrastructure, and separating individuals with diabetes from other clients during clinic days, as well as the use of technology, will go a long way to enhance education on clinic days [39, 40].

This study reveals a fundamental misunderstanding of the chronic nature of diabetes on the part of the participants. A large number of participants in this current study, as a result of a lack of knowledge, indicated that they would rather keep information on their diagnosis and management, including glucose monitoring, to themselves than share it with anyone besides their close family members (spouse, children, and sibling). Some do this for the avoidance of stigmatisation, while others think it is not necessary because they may not lose or benefit anything from such individuals they will be disclosing it to. This paints a clear picture that there is a significant element of stigma and a desire for privacy associated with newly diagnosed T2D. This limits the potential for broader community support. It suggests that support interventions need to be sensitive and confidential, perhaps focusing on the immediate family unit as the first point of contact.

This finding is comparable to Kohinor (2011), who found the main factors militating against the disclosure of information to include cultural practices, shame, gossip, stigmatisation, and social disgrace [41]. Alrasheed and colleagues (2022) also found that nondisclosure of information was significantly higher among individuals with type 2 diabetes than those with type 1 diabetes. Some individuals with diabetes in their study were also found to be hiding some glucose readings from providers [42], which is not the case in this study. This study focused only on individuals with type 2 diabetes; hence, it could not have compared with other types of diabetes. This study, however, revealed in more detail that newly diagnosed individuals see no need to disclose their condition to third parties, but they do disclose it to close family members whom they think could be of help to them.

One revelation from this study that points to a lack of knowledge by the participants is the kind of errors they committed. This study found that individuals newly diagnosed with T2D commit errors pertaining to their glucose monitoring which could have been avoided if it was not at the initial stages after diagnosis or if they had some kind of experience or knowledge about their condition before data collection. Some of the errors committed that could have been avoided included missing clinic appointments after seeing that their sugar level has been normalised. They see a normal reading as a cure or a reason to disengage, not as evidence that their current management plan is working. Secondly, they were unable to identify the signs of hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemia, unable to detect side effects of medication and mistaking side effects of medication for signs of hyper and hypoglycaemia and vice versa.

This indicates a lack of practical, actionable knowledge. Individuals newly diagnosed with T2D were not equipped to interpret their body’s signals correctly. This is dangerous because they might undertreat a dangerous hypo- or hyperglycaemic event or stop taking necessary medication due to misunderstood side effects. It shows that education must be simple and repetitive and focus on symptom recognition.

These findings were found to be contrary to the findings of several studies where participants were found to have good awareness and adequate knowledge regarding signs of complication and medication side effects [43]. For instance, Das and colleagues (2024) found that most individuals with diabetes mellitus had a fair understanding of hypoglycemia and recommended that care providers should still offer more education [44]. These contradictions might emanate from the fact that these previous studies were all conducted on clients who were diagnosed for over a year and beyond and might have gotten some experience and education from care providers. Methodologically, most of these previous studies were also quantitative and might not have captured the in-depth experience of the participants.

### Social and environmental determinants of glucose monitoring

The findings of this study revealed some social and environmental factors affect participants’ adherence to glucose monitoring, which include lack of access to monitoring equipment, untrusted results, cost of strips, and fear of needle prick, among others. It was found that most of these newly diagnosed individuals did not have personal glucometers and either had to pay for it at a private pharmacy or were forced to wait until it was time for review. The few that had glucometers also complained about the cost of procuring strips. These challenges push most of them not to monitor their glucose level regularly. Based on these challenges, it was clear that the majority of the clients were not adhering to regular glucose monitoring as a lifestyle modification measure.

This is a primary structural barrier. Knowledge is useless without the tools to act on it. Participants were seen to be making rational economic choices between feeding their family and buying test strips. This finding directly links health outcomes to poverty and access, moving the problem beyond individual responsibility and into the realm of public health policy.

These findings are consistent with several other studies. Nguyen and colleagues (2020) found that only 26% of participants and in other jurisdictions only 8.5% were adhering to regular glucose monitoring for fear of needle pricks and other factors. They only check their glucose level if they are feeling uncomfortable or unwell [9, 10]. Though the findings are in line with this current study, there are variations in the methodology used for both studies. Kofi and colleagues (2023), Adu and colleagues (2024), and Afaya and colleagues (2020) all consistently found adults with T2D to have poor glycaemic control [13, 14, 16]. The only contrary finding was in Iraq, where about 64% of participants were found to be adhering to regular monitoring of their glucose levels [11]. This discrepancy may be due to differences in methodology, culture, and geographical location of participants. The economic situation of the area and the individuals involved is a major factor here. The area had a limited number of facilities where one could easily access these services. The individuals were also mostly economically dependent on others, making it difficult for them to regularly fund the cost of monitoring as required.

### Incentives and motivational drivers shaping glucose monitoring behaviours

When it came to support systems, this study found that the majority of the participants indicated that they do not get external support in any form from anywhere, not even from their extended family except their immediate close family members. One of the factors that might have accounted for this is the fact that most of them were reluctant to discuss their situation with their extended family members for fear of stigmatisation, misconception, information spread, or gossip, and for the perception that they will not benefit anything by doing so. This perception could also be true because most of their relatives were equally not economically stable enough to support others. These findings suggest that most newly diagnosed individuals deal with their condition mostly without support. Almost all participants were not aware of any form of support from the government of Ghana. The only source of support for participants was from their close relatives, such as children, spouses, and sometimes pastors and formal health care providers. These findings confirm findings from previous studies where individuals diagnosed with diabetes were found to get most of their support from their families. Spouses were even found to play an important role in terms of support, including spiritual support [9, 20, 45]. Besides the physical and financial support from their families, participants also indicated that there was a lot of psychological support from formal healthcare providers and spiritual support from their spiritual leaders. This kind of support provides psychological and existential coping mechanisms. It is a crucial cultural context in Ghana because faith is a key part of the support ecosystem.

These findings are also in line with other findings in previous studies [14, 19]. This study, however, unlike previous studies, found that newly diagnosed individuals tend to deal with certain family members, whom they termed as closed, and not all family members.

Furthermore, the findings of this study also reveal that there are motivating factors that keep these individuals making it possible for them to cope with the lifestyle modification despite their sorrow and encounter with numerous challenges. Firstly, it was revealed that some participants were motivated to continue based on the fact that they have people who depend on them. In order to cater for their dependents, there is a need to remain alive and healthy. Also, some of the participants were also hoping to get well one day at a point where lifestyle modification would no longer be necessary, and this was enough to keep them adhering to their treatment regimen. Similarly, some participants had their hope in a divine intervention; they felt they needed to help themselves first in order for God to also help them, though they did not attribute the cause of their condition to any spirituality. Findings from Mohamed and colleagues (2020) established the fact that there are motivating factors for individuals with T2D that push them to change and adhere to modification measures [23]. In China, it was found that some participants were motivated by the fear of death and the fact that they did not want to have complications that might affect their economic independence. Being economically dependent and unable to carry out certain activities for oneself, including self-care practices, leads one to become a burden on others. Knowing this, some of the participants express their desire not to be burdensome to their family members, hence a motivating factor to adhere to the treatment regimen, including glucose monitoring as a lifestyle modification measure [23]. The findings of this current study, however, show that most participants were not worried about becoming burdensome to their families because most of their family members were not in the know of their condition and were not offering any support except their very close family member. Participants were rather thankful to their immediate families for the support, feeling that as a family, it is only normal to support each other. Similar to the findings by Mohammed and colleagues (2020), this study also revealed that participants in this current study were motivated by the fact that they did not want to die, leaving their dependents [12].

In another vein, the findings in this study also showed that some participants had their motivation from the positive results they got by adhering to lifestyle modification. Seeing changes internally and feeling better was enough for some participants to adhere to lifestyle modifications, including glucose monitoring. Some express happiness seeing their sugar level getting normal and want to do more to keep it as such. This is a vital insight into human motivation. People are motivated by visible progress and positive reinforcement. It provides a reason for healthcare workers to always show individuals diagnosed with T2D their management progress as a powerful tool to encourage adherence, even when it is difficult.

Some participants, however, tend to miss clinic appointments upon realising that their sugar level normalises by stopping the monitoring process, stopping the medication, and staying away from the clinic review.One other motivating factor found by Mohammed and colleagues (2020) was participants observing that other clients achieved positive results [23]. Comparatively, this is contrary to the findings of this current study. The difference is that participants in this current study were motivated by their own positive results, while in that of Mohammed and colleagues, participants were motivated by observing the positive results of other clients.

Some of the participants also agreed that they draw some form of motivation from their close family members. The support they get from these relatives makes them obliged to play their part by adhering to the modifications. Besides their family members, others also try to adhere because of the words of encouragement and praise they get from care providers when they come for review with good results.However, the challenge is that these systems are likely not communicating with each other, creating a fragmented support experience for the patient.

This finding is also in line with findings by Mohammed and colleagues, who affirm the importance of family support and inner motivation by further stating that knowledge alone is not enough to ensure adherence to lifestyle modification, but with support and self-motivation [12, 23].

In conclusion, these findings suggest that the experience of being newly diagnosed with T2D is overwhelming. Individuals affected receive complex information without adequate foundational education. Their management, especially glucose monitoring, represents tasks that come with fear of stigma and financial crippling. Their non-adherence is not a character flaw but a rational response to an impossible set of circumstances. Their behaviour of avoiding clinics and not testing is a form of avoiding the stress and cost associated with it.

To answer the research question, the experiences of individuals newly diagnosed with T2D are characterised by the following: fear of stigma and commission of errors due to a lack of understanding of the disease’s chronic nature and its symptoms, financial challenges due to the overwhelming burden of cost which shapes their monitoring behaviours, and privatisation of their management, where it is kept within a very small, trusted circle due to stigma. Additionally, they also experience fragmented support. While support exists from family, spiritual leaders and formal care providers, these systems operate in silos, leaving significant gaps. These individuals were also found to need positive reinforcement since they were motivated by seeing tangible success.

### Limitations of the study

This study is subject to the general limitations of qualitative research enquiries, such as researcher influences leading to some biases; however, the researcher took measures to try to mitigate this by ensuring trustworthiness. Also, any unforeseen unique or new experiences that could have emerged when the sample size had been expanded or selected by a random probability method are considered a limitation of this study. However, the sample size was also enough to ensure an in-depth appreciation of the experiences of individuals newly diagnosed with T2D in lifestyle modification. Finally, this study specifically investigated experiences related to type 2 diabetes; the findings are context-specific and therefore limited and may not be appropriate to extrapolate to individuals with other types of diabetes.

## Conclusion and recommendation

In conclusion, this study revealed that, when it comes to glucose monitoring, individuals newly diagnosed with T2D due to lack of knowledge tend to avoid clinic appointments for review upon realising their glucose level normalises. They also, as part of their experiences, sometimes mistake signs of hypoglycaemia, hyperglycaemia, and side effects of medication for each other. These individuals also found it difficult to disclose their glucose monitoring status to others except their very close relations, such as children and spouses. They were found not to be adhering to regular glucose monitoring, which they attribute to cost and lack of access. They see cost as the number one challenge to their glucose monitoring adherence. Their source of support usually comes from their close relatives, spiritual leaders, and formal care providers. Recording decreasing figures when monitoring glucose was found to be a motivating factor. The findings of this study paint a picture of a challenging journey for individuals newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes in the setting. Their core experiences are characterised by a knowledge gap that is exacerbated by significant socioeconomic barriers, such as cost and access, and moderated by limited support systems. Newly diagnosed individuals are caught between the willingness to manage their disease and the practical difficulty of managing it perfectly. This results in poor glucose monitoring practices that appear rational from their perspective but are harmful from the clinical perspective.

The researchers recommend, firstly, an intensification and development of targeted educational programmes to improve the understanding of individuals affected. Secondly, the Ghana Health Service should also partner with Non-governmental Organisations (NGOs) or private insurers to ensure subsidised cost and availability of essential medication and glucose monitoring materials. Thirdly, the facility managers can also introduce case managers to provide follow-ups, create peer-support networks, or mentorship programmes for affected individuals. Finally, future studies are recommended to use quantitative methods in order to quantify how these experiences of cost, access to care, and lack of support, among others, affect these individuals.

## Abstract

### Background

Diabetes has become a significant public health concern due to its global prevalence rate of 11.1%. Type 2 diabetes (T2D) alone accounts for 90% of all cases. The situation is worse in Africa due to the poor diagnostic systems. In Ghana, the condition affects over 2.4 million people, with the Upper East Region, which used to be one of the lowest in terms of diabetic cases, beginning to record new cases daily.

### Objective

To explore the experiences of individuals newly diagnosed with T2D on glucose monitoring and support systems availability, and motivating factors for them to continue to adhere to their glucose monitoring as a lifestyle modification measure.

### Methods

A qualitative, exploratory design was employed, targeting individuals diagnosed with T2D within the 6 months preceding data collection. A purposive sampling technique was used to recruit 15 participants. An in-depth face-to-face interview was conducted individually using a semi-structured interview guide. The data were transcribed and analysed using a thematic analysis approach.

### Results

The results revealed the emergence of 3 main themes and 8 subthemes. The main themes include the implications of knowledge deficiency on glucose monitoring, social and environmental determinants of glucose monitoring, and incentives and motivational drivers shaping glucose monitoring behaviours. Some of the key findings indicate that individuals diagnosed with T2D lack knowledge, which has negative implications for their glucose monitoring practices, including the commission of avoidable errors and not disclosing information about their condition and its management to others. Their main source of support was found to be mainly from close relatives. Checking and getting improved results was motivating to them.

### Recommendation and conclusion

The study revealed that individuals newly diagnosed with T2D lack knowledge pertaining to glucose monitoring. They primarily receive support from close family members and are encouraged when their results improve.It is recommended that care providers and authorities intensify education on the need for regular glucose monitoring. Further studies to quantify how these experiences of lack of support and knowledge affect clients are also recommended.

## Background

The global prevalence rate of diabetes is estimated to be about 11.1% [1, 2]. According to the International Diabetes Federation (IDF), over 589 million adults aged 20 to 79 are estimated to be living with diabetes [2]. It is projected that by the year 2050, this figure is likely to rise to 853 million [3]. It is also estimated that, globally, US$1.0153.4 trillion is spent on the disease annually [2], yet 3.4 million people still die from it [1]. It is also said that 252 million people are living with undiagnosed diabetes [2]. China is said to be leading the global chart in diabetes with over 148 million cases, followed by India with 90 million [3]. Type 2 diabetes (T2D), which accounts for over 90% of all diabetic cases, is a rapidly growing public health concern worldwide, contributing significantly to morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs [2].

In Africa, 24.6 million people are living with the disease at a prevalence rate of 5% and that of undiagnosed diabetes at 72.6% against the global rate of 42.8%, and this is due to the poor diagnostic systems and lack of access to health facilities [4]. Although the prevalence rate in Africa appears low compared to the global rate, it is projected to increase to 59% by 2050. Egypt is said to be leading in terms of the prevalence of diabetes in Africa at a rate of 22.4% [2].

In Ghana, the prevalence rate is estimated to be between 2.6 and 9%, affecting 6% of adults [5]; other studies also estimate it to be at 10% [6]. According to the Ministry of Health in Ghana (MOH), about 200,000 cases of diabetes are reported at the Outpatient Department of health facilities annually [5], and about US$500 to 1000 million dollars is spent on the disease in Ghana annually [2]. The Western Region of Ghana recorded the highest number of diabetic cases in the year 2023, with the Upper East Region being one of the lowest [4]. However, statistics from the Health Information Unit of the Bolgatanga Regional Hospital, the main referral facility in the Upper East Region, indicate a surge in new cases of diabetes in 2024 [7].

Glucose monitoring is a cornerstone for effective management of diabetes; therefore, it is one of the most important lifestyle modification measures in glycaemic control [8]. It becomes necessary during the third to fifth line of treatment in managing T2D individuals [2]. At the third line of treatment, the client is put on self-management education and support (DSMES) and also empowered to manage their condition, including daily glucose monitoring for long-term success. On the fourth line of treatment, they are put on regular glucose monitoring for long-term glycaemic control while monitoring for any complications [1]. Despite the importance of glucose monitoring, newly diagnosed individuals often lack the knowledge, skills, or motivation to monitor consistently [8]. A review of existing literature showed that there is limited research exploring how individuals in the early stages of diagnosis perceive and adopt glucose monitoring, especially in the context of their broader support systems and motivators.

In Taiwan, a study revealed that only 13% to 26% of adults were able to control their blood sugar levels due to the challenges involved in adhering to self-care lifestyle modification [8]. In China and Vietnam, for instance, there have been studies on glucose monitoring where the majority reported psychological stress and exhibited poor glucose monitoring behaviours [9, 10]. Findings in other parts of the globe, such as Iraq, however, report encouraging glucose monitoring behaviours [11]. In Africa, glucose monitoring was found to be tedious in Nigeria [12]. The story is similar in Ghana, where most studies found glucose monitoring and control among individuals with diabetes to be poor [13, 14].

On the other hand, forms of support available to individuals with diabetes also play an essential role in enabling them to adhere to their management [15]. Societal, family, and healthcare support are very important in the self-management of diabetes [16]. Individuals newly diagnosed with diabetes are particularly vulnerable to emotional distress, information overload, and feelings of isolation at the initial stages after their diagnosis [17, 18]. Therefore, understanding the availability and effectiveness of support systems at this stage is very important in order to improve treatment outcomes.

Several studies appeared to suggest that support available for individuals with diabetes is mostly from their families and their care providers [19, 20]. For instance, in Kathmandu Valley in Nepal, counselling to individuals with diabetes by pharmacists was found to play an important role in glucose monitoring [21]. Spouses and relatives of individuals diagnosed with diabetes were also found to play an important role in supporting their spouses [12]. In Ghana, it was also found that mobile phone usage by care providers to emphasise lifestyle modification was a good form of support to individuals with diabetes [22].

Furthermore, studies reviewed attributes motivating factors for individuals with diabetes to include: the fear of death, the need to be economically independent, among others [23, 24]. Therefore, understanding what drives newly diagnosed individuals can help healthcare providers tailor interventions. Additionally, several studies have found that behavioural change is influenced by both internal and external motivators [19, 25,26,27]. Existing literature often focuses on individuals with long-term diabetes [28,29,30,31,32], leaving a gap regarding those newly diagnosed individuals. Meanwhile, the early post-diagnosis phase is the best teachable moment, where they may be more receptive to education and behaviour change [33]. Investigating this group’s specific motivators and barriers provides an opportunity to design timely, personalised, and effective interventions that could improve long-term disease outcomes.

According to available literature, uniqueness in cultural, economic, or other related factors also influences individuals’ experiences with lifestyle modification measures, including glucose monitoring and access to support and others [13]. Some studies suggest that individuals with low incomes or living in low-income areas experience numerous barriers in lifestyle modification management [13, 20]. The Upper East Region may have unique cultural, economic, or health system-related barriers that influence glucose monitoring and support systems. However, there is a lack of context-specific research in existing literature exploring these dimensions among newly diagnosed T2D individuals, which limits the effectiveness of generalised interventions.

Furthermore, Staniszewska and colleagues (2014) indicated that the measurement of quality in terms of health care has shifted from a disease-based to a client satisfaction-based approach, making patient experience data very key in evaluating patient satisfaction globally [34]. This supports the reason why this study uses a qualitative approach to ascertain an in-depth understanding of the experiences of participants.

Also, early diagnosis is said to be a critical window for intervention [30], yet many newly diagnosed individuals struggle with lifestyle changes and glycaemic control [17]. Understanding the experiences of individuals newly diagnosed with T2D will help healthcare providers develop appropriate strategies for dealing with such clients, thereby improving overall care [30], both in healthcare facilities and at home. These individuals with T2D, if able to adhere to glucose monitoring with a proper support system and motivating factors, lead to better glycaemic control, hence early recovery and less burden on the caregiver, resulting in effective saving of resources. In support of this, the International Diabetes Federation has emphasised the importance of early diagnosis and management of diabetes, highlighting several benefits, including the prevention of complications, premature deaths, and reduced management costs [2].

In conclusion, this study is essential to fill existing gaps in understanding how newly diagnosed individuals with type 2 diabetes engage with glucose monitoring, the types of support they receive or lack, and the factors that motivate them. The findings will inform patient-centred strategies and policies aimed at improving early self-management, preventing complications, and enhancing quality of life. It will further contribute to the body of knowledge in nursing and health care, which will inform policymakers on policies that will improve the management of individuals with T2D. Also, care providers can also use this knowledge to improve the quality of care for this category of clients.

The research question is: What are the experiences of newly diagnosed T2D individuals, particularly in terms of glucose monitoring and availability of support systems? The findings would provide a more comprehensive picture of what newly diagnosed T2D individuals experience at the early stage of their condition, in relation to glucose monitoring and support systems.

## Methods and materials

### Study setting

The setting for this study is the Bolgatanga Regional Hospital located in the capital town of the Upper East Region of Ghana. It serves as a referral hospital for the 15 districts in the region, some parts of the North East Region, and even neighbouring countries such as Togo and Burkina Faso. The Upper East Region has a total of 96 health facilities. The Bolgatanga Regional Hospital is the main referral centre in the region and is located specifically at Zaare. It borders the Bolgatanga Nurses Training College to the north, the Bolgatanga Girls’ Secondary School to the west, the National Communication Authority to the south, and the Bolgatanga Preparatory Model School to the east. The hospital is in partnership with various nursing and midwifery training colleges in the region to train nurses for the region and beyond. According to the Bolgatanga Regional Hospital Health Information Unit (HIU-RHB), the hospital has a staff strength of about 1,235, comprising 613 nurses, 166 midwives, and 59 enrolled nurses. The facility records 264,640 attendances annually, approximately 700 Outpatient Department (OPD) daily attendances, and about 2400 admissions annually [7]. In terms of diabetes, the facility records approximately 20 to 30 newly diagnosed individuals monthly on an outpatient basis. The facility is the major referral centre in the region; therefore, it offers all treatment modalities to diabetic clients, mostly on clinic days, which run on Tuesdays and Thursdays [7].

## Study design

The design for this study is descriptive exploratory under the qualitative approach. This design was found appropriate because the study aims at exploring people’s experiences of a phenomenon that is part of the qualitative paradigm [35]. Descriptive exploratory design is flexible enough to allow clients, guided by the researcher, to fully express themselves and bring out their inner feelings surrounding the phenomenon while also allowing the researcher to adjust their interview guide and notes where necessary.

## Study and target population

The study population included all individuals diagnosed with diabetes seeking care at the Regional Hospital in Bolgatanga. The target population of the study included individuals diagnosed with type 2 diabetes within the last six months before data collection who sought care at the Regional Hospital in Bolgatanga. Data from the Health Information Unit at the Bolgatanga Regional Hospital indicates that, on average, 350 people are diagnosed with diabetes annually [7]. This means the facility records at least 1 case of diabetes daily. These individuals with diabetes received their care at the clinic from general nurses’ medical practitioners.

## Inclusion criteria

Study eligibility required a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes within the last six months preceding data collection. The individual should be placed on a current regimen of third- to fifth-line diabetic treatment modality, which includes dietary modification, antihyperglycemic medication, and either being empowered to self-monitor their glucose level or being on long-term monitoring for glycaemic control. Participants should also have attained the legal adult age of 18 years or above and have the willingness to participate.

## Exclusion criteria

Individuals who met the inclusion criterion but were seriously ill, unconscious, or mentally unstable were excluded. Participants who had a life expectancy of less than the study duration or a comorbid condition that could seriously interfere with study participation or data interpretation, such as end-stage renal failure or severe cardiovascular disease, were also excluded.

### Sampling technique and sample size determination

The sampling technique used for this study is purposive sampling. This technique is a non-probability sampling method where the researcher, based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria as well as the purpose of the study, recruits participants to form part of the sample [36]. This study, therefore, employed this strategy as the appropriate technique to sample its participants. Data saturation was achieved following interviews with a total of 15 participants. This was a point where the researchers were no longer getting any new or different information from the previous interviews.

## Data collection tool

The data collection tool used for this study was a semi-structured interview guide, which was administered through a face-to-face in-depth interview. The guide was designed based on the objectives of this study and consisted of open-ended questions to allow the researcher to probe until in-depth information was obtained from each participant. The interview guide was developed purposely for this study and has never been used elsewhere. The interview guide is attached as a supplementary file for reference.

To avoid misinterpretation, the interview was recorded using a tape recorder, and field notes were taken in order to capture the gestures, mood, and other sign languages of participants. Each interview was transcribed before carrying out the next interview.

## Pilot test of data collection tool

Prior to the main data collection, the interview guide was pretested at Bongo District Hospital to ascertain the suitability of the questions. This was done on a small group of individuals, 4 in number, with characteristics similar to the target participants. Insights from this pilot informed minor revisions to the interview guide. Serendipitously, the pretest also gave the researchers an idea of the time frame approximately needed for each interview.

### Rigor

Rigor is a demonstrated commitment to trustworthiness, credibility, and ethical practice in the qualitative enquiry process [37]. Rigor is achieved based on several key concepts, some of which include credibility, transferability, dependability, confirmability, ethical practice, and authenticity, among others [37]. To ensure credibility, more time was spent with each transcript by reading it multiple times, and member checking was conducted by returning the transcripts to 10 out of the 15 participants to read and confirm if that was indeed what they meant in the audio recording. Participants who could not read were assisted by reading the transcript to them with interpretation where necessary. During each interview, follow-up questions were asked to clarify what participants meant. Questions were reframed to ensure participants understood them and as a way of getting in-depth information from participants. Comparison of field notes with recorded audio and comparison of participants’ demographic data with hospital data were all done to ensure credibility. Also, peer debriefing was always done by asking colleague researchers to read through the transcribed data to ensure credibility. Furthermore, to ensure transferability, a detailed description of the methodology was provided, and field notes were taken to capture participants’ feelings, actions, moods, and other nonverbal gestures during the interview. Pretesting of the interview guide was done to determine its suitability, which ensured dependability. To minimise the researcher’s bias and ensure objectivity, separating belief from fact, the researchers did not have any personal interest whatsoever while doing this study. For confirmability’s sake, none of the researchers were diabetic or care providers in the study setting. They equally did not represent the interest of any other person during the study; they had no friend or relative there who was either a participant or a care provider.

### Data collection procedures

Recruitment of participants followed ethical approval and permission from the Committee on Human Research, Publication, and Ethics and the hospital management, respectively. The study targeted individuals who had attended the hospital’s diabetic clinic on clinic days to seek care. All clients who were in the waiting area to be attended to were addressed by the data collection team. They were informed about the reason for our presence and were encouraged to participate in the study, indicating the benefits and any possible disadvantages.

Interested participants were made to fill out a participant recruitment form that captured their initials (identity), contact, address, age, diagnosis status (how long the client has been diagnosed), mental status, and language of preference. These details were all checked against patient records in the facility’s system to confirm if they met the inclusion criteria. All 21 individuals who met the inclusion criterion were made to consent to participate in the study by signing or thumb-printing the consent form.

Time, location, and language convenient to the participant were then arranged, and a face-to-face interview was conducted with them one after the other. Some participants were interviewed at a designated consulting room at the facility; others preferred and were interviewed at their workplace because of their busy schedules, while others were interviewed in the comfort of their homes due to a lack of means to get to the facility. They were guided to fill in their particulars, and the probing was geared towards the objectives of the study. The interviews were done one after the other until in-depth information was obtained from each participant. The in-depth interview sessions were conducted in a conversational mode with privacy, and participants were prompted with follow-up questions to ascertain a clearer understanding of their experiences. Each of the participants was assigned a unique code from ‘C1’ to ‘C15’, where ‘C’ stands for ‘client’ and 1 to 15 indicates the number of participants interviewed, for the sake of anonymity. This meant 6 qualified participants were not interviewed because data saturation had been reached after interviewing the 15th participant. The language was, however, limited to what the researchers could understand and interpret, which included English, Twi, and Gurune. Even though participants were allowed to speak any of these three languages, none of them opted to speak Twi; 9 of them spoke Gurune, and 6 of them spoke in English. The Gurune recordings were always translated into English before transcription, which was done for every interview before the subsequent ones. One of the researchers who understands, speaks, and writes in Gurune translated the audio in Gurune into English. All Gurune-spoken transcripts were member-checked to ensure the translation was accurate and credible. The data collection lasted for 5 weeks, and each interview lasted for 25 to 45 min. Field notes were always taken on other forms of communication that could not be captured by the audio recorder, such as non-verbal clues, changes in voice tone, wiping tears, participants remaining silent for a while before answering certain questions, and facial expressions. There was no repeated interview.

### Data analysis

Data analysis was done using the thematic analysis approach as described by Braun and Clarke [38]. Data from clients who spoke in Gurune were translated into English before transcription. Each audio was played and listened to by the researchers repeatedly and was transcribed verbatim back-to-back to get a transcript. As described by Braun and Clarke in their first step, printed transcripts and field notes were read through over and over again several times to make the researchers become familiar with the content of each transcript.

Secondly, the three researchers reflected on the emerging issues to get meaning from them while still linking them to the data source. Initial codes were generated by assigning codes to meaningful segments. This was done by reading the transcript line by line and marking notable issues using different colours of ballpoint pen highlighters. Meaningful and similar statements were extracted by shading them with the same colours.

Thirdly, the researchers began to search for themes where these statements with their meanings assigned with codes were now sorted and broadly categorised into potential themes, making use of a coding table.

In the fourth step, the researchers review the potential themes by critically examining each code and either combining, separating, or regrouping them. Some of the codes were also discarded.

In the fifth step, the researchers review and concisely name the generated themes.

Finally, in the sixth step, the report was written with an interpretation of the findings and supporting literature.
